entries.title: Prompt-cache TTL per agent role
entries.brief: Shuttle sets the prompt-cache TTL per role: 1 hour for the driver and Webster Master, 5 minutes for the rest
entries.body:
Claude Code gives a subscription's main session a 1-hour prompt-cache TTL (cache write 2× base input) and subagents/forks 5 minutes (1.25×); every lyx agent is a main session in tmux, so all of them write at the 1-hour price (see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md).

Measured on the `landing` run's transcripts: Discussion, Plan, Bouncer and Burler never paused more than 90 s between turns, so 5 minutes keeps them warm; ly-drive paused up to 508 s (three gaps over 5 minutes), so it needs 1 hour.

## Decision (operator, 2026-10-07)

- 1 hour: the driver and Webster Master.
  Since card batching, one fork implements several cards, so the master idles well past 5 minutes while it waits on a batch.
- 5 minutes: every other role.

## Shape

Shuttle sets `CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL=5m|1h` (Claude Code v2.1.242+) per role when it spawns a session, configurable per role, with the split above as the default.
loomyard was developed with the 5-minute limit in mind, so 5 minutes matches its design assumption.

entries.title: Convergence: measure hub and driver interventions, fix at the source, hardening freezes
entries.brief: Plan for lyx to converge rather than accumulate bugs: per-run intervention log, real-wiring tests, feature freezes
entries.body:
Operator 2026-09-30: take a step back and plan for convergence, not keep accepting more bugs.
Observed today: nearly every hub intervention was in same-day new code (#319: approve nil dep, reject reading its file argument as run-id), and both passed tests built on fake deps.
Ingredients: (1) log every hub intervention and ly-drive repair per run with a class and cause, so interventions per run and new-vs-repeat failure classes are visible; (2) every fix at the source with a test that drives the real CLI wiring, not only fakes; (3) freeze periods with no new verbs or recipe rows, hardening only, until the intervention rate flattens.
Goal: the outside LLM steps in rarely, and for the task rather than for lyx.
## Model trial (from `model-spec-short-form`, operator 2026-10-01)

Try `fable[high]` for discussion and review, where design judgement matters (refusal-audit's holes came from opus Discussion and opus reviews; a Fable review found the design problem), and keep sonnet for implementation.
Change it only between runs, and measure review rounds, PR rejects and interventions before and after.

## Friction on halt

Moved to task `agent-self-reflect` (operator, 2026-10-03).

entries.title: An MCP server over lyx exposing the verbs agents need
entries.brief: A few coarse MCP tools over lyx, chosen by measured agent use and exposed per role, so agents see typed schemas instead of guessing CLI shapes
entries.body:
## Why

Agents misuse or bypass lyx (the hub read `_board/*.json` with jq) because the CLI shape is not discoverable.
An MCP tool carries a typed input schema and a description.

## Constraint from the operator (2026-10-01)

Not one tool per verb: MCP entries are heavy.
Only the important ones are exposed, and how to pick them is still open.

## Proposed selection

1. **Measure first.** Mine transcripts and logs for which lyx commands agents run, where they fail, and where they read around lyx.
2. **Few coarse tools.** One tool per area with an `action` enum (the pattern of Claude Code's Artifact tool), e.g. `board`, `run` (status, approve, reject), `webster` (Master only); a handful in total.
3. **Per-role exposure.** A fork may get none, Master gets `webster`, the hub gets `board` and `run`.

## Shape

- A thin server shipped in the ly plugin; each action calls the same module seam the CLI uses, so behaviour never forks.
- The CLI stays for humans and scripts.
- Wins: no shell-quoted JSON payloads, and per-tool permissions (an agent can be denied `accept-audit`).

Related: `bolt-roadmap-tiers`, `process-naming`.


## Status: needs a careful design session first

Operator 2026-10-01: what goes into the MCP must be thought through very carefully; this is not a loom task yet.
Questions for that session:

- Which verbs need an MCP tool at all, and which are served well enough by a better `--help` (payload schema and an example per command) and a per-role command card in each stencil, generated from the cobra tree?
- Is permission gating (an agent denied `accept-audit` or `approve`) the real reason for MCP, since `--help` and cards cannot give it?
- One tool per module was raised and judged too heavy (long descriptions); what is the cut instead?

entries.title: creel: the one way to reach an agent
entries.brief: Post (pulled mail with reminders), inject and interrupt to any agent by name, through one daemon per hub; built standalone first, then wired in two stages
entries.body:
Creel is the one module anything uses to reach an agent: a Go program, another agent or the operator in a terminal.
Every agent in lyx runs through shuttle and lives in a reed strand, so every agent has an address (`agent-naming`'s `<shortname>:<slug>:<role>`).
The decisions below are the operator's of 2026-10-06 and govern; the 2026-09-20 design under History is superseded where it differs.

## Why

Claude's `SendMessage` lands straight in the orch session, past the orch watcher, so nothing holds it during a context cycle.
A message that arrives while the orch writes its note is seen, but the note request says to write and end the turn, so it is lost at `/clear` unless the note happens to carry it.
A message that arrives after the note is written starts a turn whose end opens the clear gate, so that turn's work never reaches the note.
Batten notices do not have this problem: they go through the watcher's notice queue (`orchengine.QueueNotice`, `.lyx/orch/notices/`), which holds them during a cycle.
Every message goes through creel instead, agent to agent and module to agent alike, and the watcher's notice queue folds into creel.

## Decisions (operator, 2026-10-06)

### Verbs: one module, separate verbs per guarantee

- `lyx creel post <receiver> "<text>"`: mail. Stored in the receiver's mailbox; the receiver is reminded until it reads it.
- `lyx creel inject <receiver> "<text>"`: typed straight into the receiver's pane as its next input, once the receiver is idle. For commands (`/clear`, `/compact`, the reload) and creel's own reminder lines; anything the receiver must read and answer is `post`, not `inject`. No read receipt. Only privileged senders may inject into another strand; injecting into one's own strand is free.
- `lyx creel inject --interrupt <receiver> "<text>"`: interrupt the receiver's running turn, wait until it is idle, then type the text: "stop, and do this instead".
- `lyx creel interrupt <receiver>`: stop the receiver's running turn without killing its pane. It bypasses the queue, since it must act while the receiver is busy.
- `lyx creel forward <message-id> <receiver>`: move an unread message, envelope and body, to another receiver's mailbox; nothing stays behind in the forwarder's. The id is creel's, shown by `inbox` and in the reminder line (such as `#41`). Its `from` stays the original sender and the envelope's `path` gains the forwarder, so the message records the whole way it has taken (sender, then each forwarder in order) and the new receiver replies to the sender, not to whoever forwarded it. The forwarder need not read the body: the reminder line carries each message's sender and a short subject (its first line), enough to route. Creel knows nothing of why a message is forwarded (see `run-message-routing`, where a run's driver routes instructions to the agent working in its run).
- `lyx creel read`, `lyx creel inbox`, `lyx creel log`: below.

The operator deals with creel only.
No other module offers a verb that types into an agent's pane: `lyx shuttle send` and `lyx shuttle interrupt` move behind creel when it is wired (stage 2 or 3).

### Layering

`creel → shuttle → reed → tmux`, each layer owning one thing:

- **creel** decides what is delivered and when: the queue per receiver, priority (an inject goes ahead of mail reminders), holding, the journal and read status.
- **shuttle** knows the LLM: whether its session is idle (`IdleProbe`), and how text and keys reach it safely (paste, submit, the interrupt key). Creel asks shuttle and owns no idle probe itself. Shuttle knows nothing of queues or senders and exposes no send verb.
- **reed** knows which pane a strand lives in and does the keystrokes (`SendText` for literal text, `SendKey` for named keys such as Escape).

`PATTERN-orch-pane-single-writer` becomes: only creel decides what is delivered into an agent's pane.

### Mail is pulled

- `post` puts the message in the receiver's mailbox, and creel injects one short line, such as `[creel] 2 unread from ly:x:driver, ly:batten`.
- The line repeats each time the receiver goes idle, until it runs `lyx creel read`; only then is the message marked read. So "delivered" means "read", and creel knows it for certain.
- A busy receiver need not read at once: it knows it has mail and picks it up when it is done. An orch close to a context cycle leaves its mail unread, and creel reminds it after the cycle.
- No extra turn: the reminder starts a turn and the agent reads within it.
- A long message is a file the sender writes, and the mail says which file to read.

### Reading

- `read`: the oldest unread message, together with every other unread message from the same sender.
- `read --from <sender>`: every unread message from that sender.
- `read --all`: every unread message.
- `inbox`: the senders with their unread counts.

### Holding

A sender may hold mail reminders to a receiver and release them later.
The orch watcher holds `ly:orch`'s reminders during a context cycle, while its own messages still pass: the note request (post) and `/clear`, `/compact` and the reload (inject).

### The note request is mail (operator, 2026-10-07)

The watcher posts the note request to `ly:orch` rather than injecting it, so the orch reads it when it is ready and is never interrupted mid-work.
The orch replies by post: `written <path>` once the note is written, or `defer`.
An injected request has no receipt: on 2026-10-07 the operator dismissed one at the prompt, the watcher counted it as delivered and waited silently until its timeout, and later `distill` requests queued behind it.
With post the watcher's timeout tells two cases apart:

- Unread: the orch has not seen the request; creel keeps reminding it at each idle.
- Read but unanswered: the orch saw it and did not reply; the watcher gives up and shows the reason in `lyx orch status` and reed.

A dismissed request is answered with `defer`, never left unanswered.

### Receivers

- An unknown name is refused, listing the names that exist.
- A known receiver that is dead or dormant keeps its queue, and delivery resumes when its strand is live again.
- A receiver whose strand is removed (a producer's agent ending, for one) leaves no mail behind unread: each unread message goes one step back along its `path` (operator, 2026-10-07): to the last forwarder, or to the sender when it was never forwarded, marked with the receiver that ended without reading it, so it can be routed again. When that step is gone too, it goes on up the path towards the sender; when the sender is gone or external, the message is marked undelivered and stays in the journal. Creel learns only that the strand no longer exists, never why: the daemon sweeps the pool (below) on each tick for unread messages whose holder is no longer a strand, so no event is needed when a strand dies.
- A terminal is never typed into: what is typed into a shell is a command. A terminal or program that wants an answer waits on creel's socket instead (`post --wait-reply`, `read --wait`) and prints it.

### Daemon and transport

- A creel daemon of its own per hub, apart from reed's watchdog, since reed must not depend on creel. It owns the queues, the reminders and the read status.
- It listens on a Unix socket named by the hub's shortname, such as `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/lyx/creel-<shortname>.sock`, acknowledges receipt, and is started by any creel verb that finds it down, as `lyx reed` starts its tmux server.
- The sender is named from the environment: `LYX_STRAND_NAME` for a strand in reed, and a name the caller passes for a Go program.
  Anything else (a terminal, or a Claude session started outside reed) is `<shortname>:EXTERNAL`, such as `ly:EXTERNAL`: upper case, so it never collides with a strand name, and it claims only what creel knows, that the sender is not a strand.
  The envelope adds what creel can see of an external sender: its terminal, the process that ran the verb (`claude`, `bash`) and its directory, shown as `from ly:EXTERNAL (claude, pts/4, ~/Code/…)`.
  An external sender has no address, so a reply reaches it only through `--wait-reply`.
- A Claude session the operator adds to reed by hand (`lyx reed add --name explore --cmd claude`) is a strand with an address, though shuttle did not start it; shuttle's idle check must work on such a pane too, and stage 1 tests it.
- A filesystem drop-box (sender writes a file into the receiver's queue directory) was set aside: several writers in one directory, and no receipt for the sender.

### Storage

- One pool per hub, not a mailbox per receiver (operator, 2026-10-07): every message is stored once with its id, its sender and its current holder, so `forward` only changes the holder, and a sweep finds every message whose holder is gone.
- Access follows the holder: `read` and `forward` work only on messages the caller holds, so "read" always means the holder read it and no agent reads another's mail by mistake or by guessing an id. A sender may see the status of its own messages (read, by whom), never take them back.
- JSONL files under the hub's `.lyx/creel/`, written only by the daemon.
- Unread messages stay until read; read messages and journal lines are deleted after 7 days, so a week of traffic stays available for debugging.
- The journal holds one line per event (posted, reminded, read, injected, interrupted), and `lyx creel log` shows it.

### Later, not stage 1

- Sending across hubs is a feature of its own. The address already picks the hub's socket, so it costs nothing in stage 1.
- An MCP layer on top of the verbs, if an agent outside a terminal ever needs one.

## Build in stages (operator, 2026-10-06)

Creel is a new module that every delivery will depend on, so it is built and tested standalone before anything is wired to it.
Each stage below becomes its own task when creel is promoted.

1. Creel alone: the daemon, the queues, the journal, every verb above, and delivery through shuttle gated on the receiver being idle, tested against fake panes and in the tmux tier. No other module sends through it yet; the operator tries it from a terminal.
2. System notices: the orch watcher's and batten's notices and the watcher's injects go through creel, and the watcher's notice queue and idle probe go. The watcher keeps only its cycle logic (tracking tokens, choosing `refresh`/`distill`/automatic cycles, waiting for the note, sequencing the reload, its state and lifecycle), and advances a cycle phase only on the orch's reply to the note request, or once creel confirms a command inject was typed.
3. Agents: the parent-review gate (`internal/parentreview/gate.go`, which today prompts Discussion-Write to `SendMessage` the parent) posts itself, drivers' stop reports post instead of duplicating batten's notices over `SendMessage`, and `lyx shuttle send`/`interrupt` move behind creel.

Fixes that do not need creel, such as `shuttle-asking-holds`, go ahead of it.

## History: the 2026-09-20 design (superseded where the decisions differ)

Deferred 2026-10-02 while Claude Code's `SendMessage` was enough; resumed 2026-10-06 for the reason under Why.
Its address grammar (`name@slug[.hub]`) is superseded by `agent-naming`'s `<shortname>:<slug>:<role>`, and its pane-title and session-name reconcile belongs to reed.

### The idea

Deliver messages/events to any Strand (agent, operator, `ly-drive` watchdog, orchestrator) by address.

### The send/receive asymmetry

Being a Strand is only required to *receive* mail — an address needs somewhere durable to deliver to. It is **not** required to *send*: anything able to reach the delivery mechanism can send without needing an address of its own. An in-process Claude Code fork subagent is the clearest example — it can never itself become a Strand (it is never an OS/tmux process), but it can still send.

### Addressing

The address format is **`name@slug[.hub]`** — the email shape, deliberately: "deliver to *name* at *place*" needs no explanation for humans or agents, and the grammar is collision-free because slugs (`[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`) can contain neither `@` nor `.`, so the single `@` splits unambiguously and the optional `.hub` suffix reads exactly like an unqualified-vs-qualified hostname (omitted = own hub).
The resemblance to real email is a known confusion risk, accepted on purpose — it buys the mental model.
Real external channels never ride on it: a raw email address is never a valid recipient, and creel never guesses whether something "is" email.
Instead — **later, not creel v1** — external channels are **connector domains**: the rule is that the rightmost element decides the router — a known hub (or nothing) means internal post, while a reserved connector domain (`slack`, `email`, …) hands *everything left of it* to that connector module to interpret (`user@slack`; possibly `orch@slug.hub.slack` if each slug gets its own Slack channel — the connector owns that mapping, creel's core never parses it).
Each connector module owns its own list of valid left-side names, and that configured list *is* the allowlist: a confused agent structurally cannot reach an arbitrary third party.
Inbound goes the same way: a reply arriving from Slack enters creel as ordinary mail with the connector address as `from`, so the receiving agent just replies to `from` and never knows Slack exists.
Connector domains are excluded from the hub-name grammar, so no hub can ever shadow one.
Resolution stays heuristic-free everywhere: a recipient resolves to a strand, or ends in a connector domain, or is refused with the list of names that exist.
Creel v1 reserves the grammar only; no connector ships with it.
(The `@` file-mention in Claude Code's interactive input is a UI autocomplete trigger only — an address in a shell argument is just text — so the overlap costs a cosmetic popup when a human types an address in the prompt box, nothing more.)

- **The strand guid is the identity; names are the address.**
  Every strand has a guid for its whole life, pane or no pane; creel resolves an address at *delivery* time (slug → session, name → strand → guid) and delivers to the guid.
  Names are what humans and agents write, because names are role-stable while guids are instance-bound:
  a torn-down-and-respawned orchestrator has a new guid but the same name, and mail to `orchestrator@task-a` should reach whoever holds the role now.
  A reply can carry the guid when pinning one specific instance matters (detecting "the one I was talking to is gone").
- **Self-identification is injected, not looked up.**
  Reed owns every spawn/relaunch command line, so it injects `LYX_REED_ID` (the guid) and `LYX_STRAND_NAME` into every process it starts.
  The full address is *derived*, never injected: worktree slug comes from the cwd resolution the process already lives under, so `<slug>:<$LYX_STRAND_NAME>` composes at the point of use — a third stored copy could only drift.
  Fallback and verification: `$TMUX_PANE` (the `%`-id, server-unique, never renumbered) joins against the state's `PaneID` field; env and join disagreeing is an anomaly worth surfacing, not just a fallback order.
  Agents should treat the injected name as their own: ly-drive and sibling stencils read `$LYX_STRAND_NAME` at session start and use it in self-reference and as sender.
- **Names mirror to pane titles for humans, authority stays in state.**
  Reed sets the tmux pane title (`select-pane -T`) to the strand name at spawn/relaunch; tmux titles are display-only and enforce nothing, so the state's name field remains the single lookup key — the same volatile-view/durable-truth split `PaneID` already has.
  Reed owns the title channel alone: `allow-set-title off` on reed-managed panes, because any program in a pane can otherwise retitle it via the OSC 0/2 escape at any time (Claude Code does, continuously), and a cooperating-agent scheme is exactly the drift vector to close, not a feature.
  The per-hub daemon's tick adds the safety net: compare each tracked pane's actual title against the strand name, rewrite on divergence, and log that it happened — reconcile, same as the rest of reed's repair machinery.
  And the hard rule that makes display drift harmless rather than merely unlikely: **delivery never resolves through a pane title** — routing is always name → state → guid, so a stale title can mislead an eye but never a message; a send to a name the state doesn't know refuses with the list of names that exist (the same refuse-with-list idiom shed's run addressing uses), which itself surfaces the drift.
  A listing verb (`lyx reed list`: name, guid, session/worktree, pane-id, actual pane title, alive/dormant, drift flagged) doubles as the address directory and the diagnostic for exactly this concern.
- **An agent's own session name is the strand name too, and the daemon owns it.**
  A Claude process in a strand carries a session name of its own (`claude --name`, `/rename`) — the name the operator sees in the session list and that session-to-session messaging addresses.
  It must equal the strand name, for the same reason the pane title must: two names set by different hands drift apart and go stale.
  Setting it once at spawn is not enough, because a Claude session's name is reset after a compact, so a long-running agent silently loses it mid-run.
  So the per-hub daemon's tick owns it as it owns the title: read each tracked agent strand's current session name, and when it differs from the strand name, restore it (e.g. `/rename <strand name>` sent into the pane at idle, the same idle-only delivery rule as mail), logging the repair.
  The strand name stays the single source of truth; the session name, like the pane title, is a mirror reed keeps in sync, never a key anything resolves through.
  "Every pane has a name" is then nearly free: everything reed spawns is a strand (the operator's terminal is Selvage, which is not a strand and so not addressable), every strand has a name, every name mirrors to its title; panes outside reed are outside the system and never routed to.
- **Rename is a relaunch.**
  Env is frozen at process start, so the name is a birth attribute set at `AddStrand` and never mutated in place — renaming a role means tearing down and respawning its strand.
- **Well-known role names make addresses guessable.**
  A small canonical vocabulary (`orchestrator`, `driver`, `operator`, …) lets an agent address `driver@<slug>` with no directory lookup at all; a listing verb covers the rest.
- **Multi-hub is out of scope, but the grammar reserves the door.**
  Operating across several repos at once would not need one reed server spanning hubs: each hub keeps its own server and per-hub daemon, and cross-hub mail becomes daemon-to-daemon relay — the optional `hub:` prefix (omitted = own hub) is the entire forward-compatibility cost, paid here in grammar only.

### Dependencies

Deliberately a separate, later task from `ly-drive + orchestrator`'s launch-convention change and the shipped `reed: born-as-strand` item, which it depends on **for the receive side only**: everything that should be addressable must already exist as a Strand before addressing it means anything. Also downstream of `worktree spawn/teardown as Shed producers`' headless-orchestration future, since a mailbox is most useful once external actors can reach a worktree without a human ever having opened it first.

### Delivery

Transport and log are two different jobs, and the terminal is bad at the second one (scrollback dies with the pane, is unsearchable, and mixes mail into everything else) — so delivery is **pull, not full-content injection**, with a durable store carrying the audit trail.

- **Every message is an envelope in the creel store**: `from`, `to`, timestamp, `kind`, status (`sent` → `delivered` → `read`).
  `from` is filled in by the send verb itself, never free-typed: derived from `$LYX_STRAND_NAME` + the cwd slug when it can be (env is inherited down the whole process tree, so Go code running inside a strand signs with the strand's address for free), falling back to the `$TMUX_PANE`-to-state join.
  Outside reed there is no address, and creel does not pretend otherwise: `from` becomes a reserved not-addressable marker (`operator`), meaning a reply is impossible and the message must stand on its own — no reply-routing is configured for the marker.
  So a receiver always knows exactly where the reply goes (or that it can't), and a sender can neither forge nor forget its identity.
  Replying is just sending to `from`.
- **Two kinds.**
  `mail` is stored and *pulled*: the receiver is notified with one short line and reads at its own pace (`lyx creel inbox` for the count, a get-one verb that flips status to `read`).
  Pulled content arrives as tool output the agent asked for — better context than a giant injected user-message — and a short fixed notification line can never break on escaping the way multi-line `send-keys` can.
  `inject` is typed verbatim into the receiving pane instead: its body is a command to *execute*, not content to read, so it never sits in an inbox — the first use case is `lyx reed self-compact`, sugar for sending `/compact` to one's own address.
  Self-injection is free; injecting into *another* strand's pane is the driver privilege, restricted to privileged senders, never something any strand can do to any other.
- **The daemon delivers, at idle.**
  Both kinds ride the per-hub daemon's existing per-tick loop (resolving the old open item — no new process): the notification line or injected body is sent-keys into the receiving pane only when the receiver is idle, not mid-turn.
- **Everything is journaled, regardless of kind.**
  An `inject` is not mail but is still logged with sender, receiver, body, and delivery time; `lyx creel log` shows all traffic hub-wide — who sent, who read, when — searchable and durable, which is strictly better backtracking than terminal scrollback ever was.
  The live-watching human still sees traffic as it happens: the notification line carries sender + subject (`2 new: watchdog@prime "loom stuck at Gate"`), bodies stay in the store.
- **Plain CLI verbs, no MCP layer.**
  Creel needs no streaming or client-side session state, so it stays ordinary `lyx` verbs like every other module; an MCP server could be layered *on top of* the same verbs later if an agent outside a terminal ever needs access — deferred until someone does, not decided against.

## Related

- the shipped `reed: born-as-strand` item — the receive-side prerequisite.
- `internal/reedengine`'s package documentation — reed's watchdog daemon, which creel's daemon stays apart from.
- `shuttle-asking-holds` — the false asking stop, fixed ahead of creel.

entries.title: Runs overview and event log in their own window in the prime session
entries.brief: An own tmux window beside the orch: one line per run on top, a log of batten notices with attach commands below; the orch notice drops its attach command
entries.body:
One screen for the operator: every run in the hub, and a running log of what happened to them.
`lyx shed status [run-id]` is per run and `lyx orch status` covers only the orchestrator, so today the hub polls each run separately and the operator sees run events only through the orch's chat.

## Where it shows

Operator 2026-10-05: its own tmux window in the prime's reed session, beside the orch's window, so the orch pane keeps its full height.
An own window also removes the 2026-10-02 problem of a status strand under the orch whose height would have to follow the number of runs.
With `reed-status-tabs`, a session with more than one window shows window tabs, and Alt+Left/Right switches between the orch and the overview.

## What it shows

- Top: one line per run with state, current producer and age.
- Below: a running event log, one line per batten notice, each with the run's attach command (`cd <pair> && lyx reed attach`), so the operator can jump into a run from it.
  Batten appends every notice to a hub log file under the prime's `.lyx`, and the window tails it.

## Notices to the orch get shorter

The `[batten notice]` line typed into the orch drops the trailing `cd <pair> && lyx reed attach`: the orch knows where a run's pair is, and the attach command is for the operator, who now gets it in the log.
`renderNotice` in `internal/battenshed/notice.go` builds that line; the orch's line and the log's line come from the same notice.

## Notice wording: a wait is not an error (operator, 2026-10-05)

Shed keeps the reason for every halt in `Status.Error`, including an awaiting PR-Gate, and `renderNotice` labels it `error:` whatever the state.
Seen: `child left running; child state awaiting, error: the pull request awaits review; …`.
Label the text by state: `error:` only for failed and blocked, and `waiting:` (or the bare reason) for awaiting and paused.
Phrase the condition by what happened, e.g. `board-config-per-worktree: awaiting at PR-Gate: the pull request awaits review`, not `child left running; child state awaiting`.

entries.title: Discussion advisor: a dedicated agent answers Discussion-Write's questions live
entries.brief: A second agent spawned beside Discussion-Write studies the task and code and answers its design questions as they arise, a real two-agent dialogue
entries.body:
- **ask mode**: Discussion-Write asks its design questions as they arise, and an answerer replies; answers to design questions, not a review.
- **The answerer is a dedicated agent**, spawned in parallel with Discussion-Write with its own prompt: it studies the task, bolt and the code while the writer drafts, so it is ready when the questions come.
  It is an address, not hard-wired to `$LYX_PARENT`; the parent is the fallback.
- Two live sessions both keep their context, so this is a real dialogue, and none of it lands in the parent's context.
  Two agents designing together beat one agent asking and answering itself.
- `ask` and `review` are independent switches: an advisor answering interview questions and the parent reviewing the draft can both run on one task.
- New machinery: one producer running two interactive sessions side by side (e.g. `ly:<slug>:discussion` and `ly:<slug>:advisor`), each waiting on the other through files; shuttle keeps an asking session non-terminal today (`internal/shuttleengine/wait.go`), which is the starting point.

entries.title: Plan cards name the members they change as glyphs, after lyx's use of glyphs is tested systematically
entries.brief: Plan-Write lists file paths instead of member glyphs because its stencil shows and allows it, and handle-unreferenced forces invented glyphs; test lyx's use of quarry glyphs systematically first
entries.body:
## Why

Seen on `gate-list`'s plan (2026-10-02): card 1's `Edit:` lists 24 file paths and no member glyph, although its Intent names the members it changes (`GateSpec`, `GateOutcome`, `Run.evaluateGate`, `resolveGateSpec`, `burlerengine#Engine.Run`).
Webster's changed-files guard then compares at file level only, no `quarry resolve` confirms the members exist, and a kick-start pack (`kick-start-pack`) has no spans to pre-resolve.

## Causes, in `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-plan.md`

- The only card skeleton shows `**Edit:**` with `` - `path/to/file.go` ``, and agents copy the shape they are shown.
- The glyph rule says a *symbol* target is spelled as a glyph and "a file path stays a plain path"; nothing says an `Edit` target should be the members changed, so a file path is always a legal choice.
- File paths are the path of least resistance: a member glyph must be looked up with `lyx quarry` and resolve at validation, and can fail as `glyph-not-found`, `glyph-ambiguous` or `containment-unit-overlap`; a file path only has to exist.
- `handle-unreferenced` requires every `plan:` handle to be used by a later card, so a new symbol only its own card uses cannot take a handle; the planner then invents a glyph (`internal/shuttleengine#GateEntry` under `Create:`), which the handle rule exists to prevent.

## Want

- The skeleton and the text say `Edit:` lists the member glyphs changed; a file path only for a file with no symbol to name (tests, non-Go files).
- The plan rubric flags an `Edit` card holding only file paths while its Intent names specific symbols.
- `handle-unreferenced` does not fire for a handle its own declaring card uses.

## First: test loomyard's use of glyphs systematically (operator, 2026-10-02, refined 2026-10-03)

The glyph library is part of quarry and the operator has tested it hard; what has failed is loomyard's own use of it (the plan stencil, the handle rules and the containment checks, in the sections below).
Before the stencil change pushes every plan onto member glyphs, test that use systematically against real plans: resolve every member glyph a sample of real cards would name, the handle bind path and the containment checks, and record what fails.

## Validation must not change verdict mid-run (2026-10-02)

Seen on `rework-generations`, batch 5: a plan valid at Plan-Write was refused at `begin-batch` with `containment-file-overlap`.
Card 4 creates `loomshed#ReworkTold` with a `plan:` handle; card 5 lists both `internal/loomshed/prrework.go` and `loomshed#ReworkTold`; card 9 lists `prrework.go`.
While the unit did not exist the handle had no location, so containment could not place it; once card 4 built it and `begin-batch` canonicalized the handle into a glyph, containment saw the overlap for the first time.
Cards 5 and 9 sit in different, sequential batches, so the overlap was harmless; the member line in card 5 was redundant beside its own file line.

Want: validation gives the same answer at Plan-Write and at dispatch.
Either containment places a `plan:` handle by its declared file at plan time, or it does not refuse overlaps between cards in different batches; and a card listing a file and a member of that same file is flagged at plan time as redundant.

## Mechanical caller coverage for deletions (seen 2026-10-03)

In `test-suite-change-amplification`'s plan the Burler found cards 36, 37 and 39 deleting helpers whose callers sit in files the cards do not list; plan-validate could not see it, because a card lists files, not the symbols it deletes or re-signs.
Once cards name deleted and re-signed members as glyphs, plan-validate can resolve every reference through quarry and flag a referencing file that no card in the same or an earlier batch edits, instead of leaving it to the Burler or to verify's compile failure.

## Priority (operator, 2026-10-06)

The operator wants this fixed soon: file-level targets waste tokens, since every agent downstream of the plan re-reads whole files to find the members a card changes.
It waits for `bugfix-webster`, whose Plan-Gate card-order checks change `internal/planglyph`.
The 2026-10-06 bugfix plans name targets by file on purpose, to survive the test prunes; that choice is not a precedent.

entries.title: Orch owns the run loop: detached batten start, a lyx watch, one land command, --continue, a committed role prompt
entries.brief: Replace the hub scratch scripts and remembered procedure with lyx itself, so an orch session runs the loop from its committed role prompt alone and resumes after a reboot
entries.body:
## Goal

An orch session runs the whole loop (start, watch, review, land, deploy) with lyx commands and its committed role prompt.
It needs no scripts in `.scratch/hub/` and no rules it must remember to read.

## Start a run detached

`lyx batten run <slug>` blocks in the foreground, so the orch backgrounds it from its own shell, and a Claude Code background job is killed at its time limit along with its process group: on 2026-10-02 all three batten runs died that way after 30 minutes.
The hub now starts them with `setsid nohup` by hand.

Starting a driver belongs in shed, not in each recipe (operator, 2026-10-05).
Today only `lyx loom start` reads a run's seed and spawns the driver it records (`--driver llm|go` on `lyx shed seed`): the detached Go runner, or an LLM strand running the driver stencil (`contracts/stencils/shed/shed-template-driver.md` once `lyx-skills-and-stencils` lands).
`lyx shed` has no such verb, so every other recipe would need its own start.

- `lyx shed start <run-id>` reads the seed and spawns the recorded driver, detached for Go (`proc.Detach`), as a reed strand for LLM, for any recipe.
- `lyx loom start` keeps its bootstrap steps (substrate, merge-in-progress refusal, parked-driver resume, terminal handover) and spawns the driver through the same code.
- `lyx batten start <slug>` is the same verb for batten's run, so a batten run survives the orch's shell without `setsid nohup`.
How the operator sees many batten runs at once (a status strand, its height, or reed's own-window anchoring) is undecided and stays out of this task.

## A watch command

Done: `orch-cycle-hardening` landed batten run notices (`[batten notice]`) that wake the orch when a run stops, its driver dies or its status goes quiet; see `internal/battenshed/notice.go` and the package's `doc.go`.

## One land command

`.scratch/hub/land.sh <slug>` plus the steps after it (pull in the prime, delete the branch on origin, `lyx board prune`) become one lyx command.
Deploy stays operator-triggered, so the command either stops before deploying or deploys only when told.

## Continue the last orch session

After a reboot the operator wants the same conversation back, as `claude --continue` gives, not a fresh session reading a handoff.
Today that takes `lyx orch start --adopt <session-id>`, with the id dug out of `~/.claude/projects/`.
`lyx orch` records its session id and offers `lyx orch start --continue` (or makes it the default for a dead strand) to adopt the last orch session.

## The orch role prompt

Moved into task `lyx-skills-and-stencils` (operator, 2026-10-05).

## Done when

- The orch starts, watches and lands runs with lyx commands only, and `.scratch/hub/` is gone.
- A started batten run survives the orch's shell and session ending.
- `lyx orch start --continue` after a reboot resumes the last orch conversation.





## How `batten start` detaches (operator and orch, 2026-10-07)

Claude Code kills the shells it starts, with their process group, after a while (about 30 minutes for a background shell), so a batten run started from the orch's shell must leave that group; today the orch uses `setsid nohup … > <log> &`, and the log it redirects to is the orch's choice, not lyx's.
Two ways for lyx to do this itself:

- A self-detaching `batten start`: it re-executes `lyx batten run <slug>` as a child in its own session (`internal/proc`'s `Detach`, `Setsid` on Linux and a new process group on Windows), with stdin from the null device and output in a log lyx owns, such as `.lyx/batten/<slug>.log`, prints the pid and log path, and exits. A lock per slug refuses a second start while a batten run for the slug is alive.
- Preferred by the operator: batten runs as a hidden reed strand (`anchor: hidden`, no pane in the layout). Reed's tmux server is outside Claude Code's reach altogether, and nobody needs to watch the process: the operator follows the runs in the prime's overview window (`runs-overview`), with the raw output kept for debugging.

entries.title: Parent-review gate: wait bound off the boundary, no mid-turn sends, live smoke
entries.brief: Close the cases the first parent-review gate left open: expiry while the writer is mid-turn, sends into a running turn after restart, poll cost, and one live smoke run
entries.body:
## Goal

The parent-review gate holds its promises in the cases the first version left open: the wait bound fires even when the writer never ends its turn, no gate send lands inside a writer turn after a restart, and a live hand-started hub is proven to receive the notice.

## From the PR #336 review (2026-10-02)

- **Live smoke.** The smoke test uses a stub writer that records the typed line, so the SendMessage hop to a real hand-started parent has never run; run it once live.
- **Wait bound off the boundary.** Expiry is checked only at a writer turn boundary (`internal/shuttleengine/wait.go`, `gateAtBoundary`), so a writer stuck mid-turn (for example on a permission prompt for `lyx loom review delivered` in interactive mode) holds the run until `discussion_timeout_min` instead of `parent_review_wait_min`; expiry needs no send, so evaluate it on every tick.
- **Mid-turn sends after a restart.** `AttachGated` replays events from offset 0, so the first tick treats the writer as idle even mid-turn: a notify-carried prompt or a reject re-prompt can be typed into a running turn, and a consumed reject is let through while the writer is still fixing.
- **Turns the loop cannot see.** A turn started by the parent replying to the writer through SendMessage, or by the operator typing, leaves the loop at a boundary; tell the orch fork not to reply to the writer.
- **Poll cost.** While pending at a boundary every 500 ms tick re-runs `discussionparser.Validate`, three locked JSON reads and a `MkdirAll`; throttle re-evaluation to a few seconds.
- **Way-forward from the prime.** The no-open-request refusal names `lyx loom status <run>`, which cannot address the child from the prime; name `lyx batten status` there.
- **`approve --review` and an empty file.** The refusal spec says it refuses a missing or empty file, the code only a missing one; align them.
- **Entry order.** `shedrecipe` does not require `parent-review` to be the gate list's last entry; a must-pass entry after it would be `not_reached` at a deadline finalize while the review is pending.
- **`delivered` after a verdict** can write `delivery.json` after the discussion commit and leave `_lyx` dirty until the next status commit.
- **Round numbers** grow on every fresh spawn with no reviewer (empty `round-N/`, never committed).
- **Review scope.** The brief says "Do not re-review the design's internal quality", narrower than millhouse's `orch-review`; confirm with the operator.

entries.title: Hardener: an autonomous behavior-review campaign that replaces crucible
entries.brief: Parked by the operator: settle the Tenter/Hardener design and build the campaign that runs a live-substrate module in a sandbox until it converges
entries.body:
## Goal

Replace `crucible`, the hand-run review-and-fix loop, with `Hardener`.
Hardener is an on-demand campaign after loom that runs a live-substrate module in a sandbox, reviews its behavior round after round, and fixes what it finds until the gates are green.
Then retire `crucible/`, which still writes to `_mill/` and runs its rounds through hand-spawned `crucible-reviewer-<effort>` agents.

## Starting point

- The design under `## Design` (DRAFT): `Tenter` is the round loop on `Treadle`, and `Hardener` is `Shed` wrapping `Tenter` with its own Preflight.
  Rounds respawn every time instead of keeping a persistent thread, and a `progress-judge` runs before and after each round.
- `crucible/README.md` is the method Hardener automates.

## Open before Discussion

- What the handoff must carry losslessly besides the finding-recurrence ledger.
- Where the line falls between the Go scaffolding and the LLM's orchestrator role.
- Whether the round agent reuses the `burler` package or only its prompt template.
- How much of the sandbox provisioning lyx automates.

## Done when

- `lyx` can start a Hardener campaign against a module and run it unattended to convergence or a round cap.
- `crucible/` is deleted, and the design's durable content lives in package docs.

## Notes

- One of the Someday items on `manifest-retire`'s triage list (`hardener`). Landing this entry removes it from that list.

## Design

> **⚠️ DRAFT. This is an early concept sketch, not a settled design.** Unlike the other module docs (which are *Design — not built* but agreed), this one is still being figured out. The shape below captures what a weekend of hand-running the method taught us and the decisions reached so far in discussion; **expect fields, mechanisms, and even the boundary of the module to change.** Do not implement from this doc yet. When the concept firms up this banner comes off and the doc becomes a normal *Design — not built* entry; per the documentation lifecycle it is eventually deleted into the package header + `overview.md` on landing.
>
> **Hand-executed origin:** `crucible` is the method this module would automate — the hand-run version of the same idea, named separately to avoid colliding with this module's own name. This was developed over the last week out of a concrete need: to **run** actual `reed` code hard enough to surface defects a green `go test` never proves. Six hand-orchestrated rounds fixed what many rounds of text-based review could not — it was genuinely *hardening*.
>
> Not required to get `loom` running — `loom` only ever uses text-review (its `Bouncer`+`Burler` review segments), never behavior-review. Kept separate from the `Treadle`/`Shed` work for exactly that reason: nothing here blocks `loom`.

## Naming: two things, not one

Two distinct layers, split out once the shared-engine design (the `internal/treadleengine` and `internal/shedengine` package documentation) was pinned:

- **`Tenter`** — the review-loop alone: `Treadle` (the generic round-loop engine — judge, gate, round-spawn, cap, pause, lock) configured with a live-substrate-driving round-runner and a behavior-review profile, instead of a `burlerengine` round + text-review profile.
  The direct structural sibling of loom's own text-review segments.
  Not separately runnable in isolation the simple way a text-review segment is, because behavior-review needs a live sandbox/worktree lifecycle around it.
- **`Hardener`** — the full, on-demand, autonomous campaign: `Shed` (the generic outer phase-FSM — see `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation) wrapping `Tenter`, plus Hardener's own Preflight (sandbox provisioning, live-suite readiness).
  This is what gets a worktree spawned for it (via `fabric`) and safe-merges back into parent when done, the same lifecycle `loom` uses, just with `Hardener`'s own producer list carrying `Tenter` where `loom`'s list carries its Discussion, Plan and Webster producers.

`Tenter` is a **behavior-based reviewer**: where a text-review segment reads an artifact, `Tenter` **runs** a live-substrate module, reacts to what it observes, and builds bespoke adversarial scenarios to break it. `Hardener` is a separate, on-demand, **post-loom** campaign — not on the `shuttle → burler → shed → loom` spine — meant to harden a live-substrate module (the archetype: `reed` driving real tmux) before merge.

## Why `Tenter` is not a text-review segment

`Tenter` and a text-review segment share the `burler` *round discipline* (see the `internal/burlerengine` package documentation) — A-review → B-fix, no self-grading, commit-per-fix, fix-everything — but they are different reviewers along two axes:

| | text-review segment | `Tenter` |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | **text** — read the artifact | **behavior** — run the module, react, build scenarios |
| Substrate | in-worktree, fast | a **live sandbox repo**; slow, heavy git/go operations |
| Gate | LLM verdict (or a light `command` gate) | **deterministic**: run the smoke suite N× concurrent, zero stray state |
| Cost | cheap, minutes | token- **and** wall-clock-heavy; a single iteration ran 1–2 hours; a campaign, a weekend |
| When | between every phase (on the spine) | **on demand, after loom**, only when `Hardener` is invoked |

A text-review segment's `command` gate lets a code profile *touch* behavior lightly;
`Tenter` is the heavy tier — driving real substrate and hand-rolling crash/rebirth/concurrency scenarios is its whole job.

## `Tenter`'s round-loop — resolved: `Treadle` drives per-round respawn, no persistent thread

**The engine underneath `Tenter` is a general one, not Tenter-specific — see the `internal/treadleengine` package documentation.**
That doc covers the round-runner interface, the judge-maintained handoff (a general improvement, not just Tenter's),
and the process for getting there (`Tenter` itself is built on `Treadle` only once `Treadle` exists).
What follows here is Tenter's own instance of that shared design.

In the hand-run version (see crucible/README.md), **one persistent orchestrator thread** stayed alive across the campaign: it spawned a fresh round agent per round, **independently verified** the round's work (re-ran the gates from cold state on the committed tree — never trusting the round's own "merge-ready" verdict), **accumulated** an understanding of where the module's bugs live, **targeted** each next round agent ("focus on X"), maintained a **handoff** that survived compaction, and asked the operator what to do next.
The targeting + accumulation is what made the reed campaign's rounds succeed where stateless text-review rounds did not — the round agent kept re-discovering the terrain cold otherwise.

**Resolved: no persistent thread.**
Go itself is the orchestrator (`Treadle`);
each round is three fresh, one-shot spawns, not a living session accumulating state in a context window:

1. **`progress-judge`, pre-round.** `Treadle` spawns a fresh one-shot agent that reads the handoff file, decides what to target next, and writes the round's seed prompt (the file the reviewer will read).
   It then terminates — no lingering session.
2. **Reviewer.** `Treadle` spawns the round agent proper, pointed at the prompt the judge just wrote — the same A-review → B-fix, commit-per-fix, no-self-grading round crucible already runs by hand.
   This is the `burler`-shaped worker;
   the *campaign* loop wrapping it is new, the round itself is not.
3. **`progress-judge`, post-round.** `Treadle` spawns a fresh one-shot agent that reads the handoff plus the round's review/fixer-report artifacts, **independently validates the findings** (crucible's non-negotiable rule — three of the reed campaign's seven rounds self-reported "merge-ready" and were wrong each time), rewrites the handoff in place, and decides whether another round is needed or the campaign has converged.

**Naming, fixed:** the pre/post role above is **`progress-judge`**, reusing the term the text-review gate's own description already uses ("run `burler` rounds → `APPROVED`/`stuck` + `progress-judge` + cap") — not "handler."
"Handler" already names a different thing in loom's existing vocabulary (the A-review→B-fix round worker itself, i.e. the "Reviewer" above) — reusing it for the targeting/validating role would collide with that.

The handoff file is the sole accumulation vehicle;
there is no live memory anywhere in the loop.
The one cost this pays versus a text-review segment today: a `progress-judge` spawn on **both** sides of the reviewer, not just post-round — a text-review segment's judge doesn't do this pre-round targeting for Discussion/Plan/Webster today;
those rounds reuse a fixed rubric, not a dynamically retargeted prompt.

### Pre-round targeting

Superseded by the `internal/treadleengine` package documentation — pre-round targeting is designed there as a general capability `Treadle`'s judge can support, exercised by Tenter's profile and simply unused by a text-review profile. See that doc's "Pre-round targeting" section instead of resolving this here.

### The handoff — two-tier memory, and the one crux

- **Handoff** — a **distilled summary**, **edited in place each round** (not appended, so per-round context stays bounded regardless of round count).
  Always read.
  The orchestrator's compressed understanding + what to target next. *(The hand-run instructions already rewrite it in place per round — this discipline is proven, not new.)*
- **Raw reviews + fixer-reports** — complete, authoritative, **read on demand** when the handoff points at something needing detail.
  Reviews inform *targeting*;
  fixer-reports inform *verification*.

The read-set is *instructions + handoff (always) + selective raw files (on demand)* — **not** "all reviews every round," which would reintroduce the O(N) context growth the handoff exists to kill.

**The one crux for going stateless (per-round respawn):** in the hand-run version a *live* thread held some things implicitly — above all "this finding has recurred before."
A respawn has no live memory, so **anything the thread knew implicitly must become explicit in the handoff.**
The prime suspect is the **finding-identity / recurrence ledger** (which findings reappeared in which rounds): if an in-place edit "cleans up" a finding that looks resolved, the recurrence trail can be silently lost and stuck-detection fails quietly.
So: **distill the prose, but keep the key-ledger lossless.**
The migration persistent-thread → respawn is essentially this one audit — find what the live thread knew implicitly and make it explicit.

### Reuse: only `Bouncer` carries over

`Tenter`'s own review-loop is expected to land as a `Shed` segment: a round producer (this module's own equivalent of the shipped `shedadapters: Burler-round producer`, wrapping whatever `Tenter`'s round mechanism turns out to be — not `burlerengine`) paired with an instance of the shipped `Bouncer: the generic review-gate producer`, the same hand-wired shape `loom`'s own review producers use (folk name "perch," see `CLAUDE.md`'s terminology note — this segment is "a perch" in that same loose sense, same shape, different round producer inside it).
Only `Bouncer` is literally reusable code here: `burlerengine`'s own round mechanism is inherently text/diff-specific (Target/Fasit/Rubric over a `shuttle` session editing text), so `Tenter`'s round producer needs its own from-scratch implementation of the same always-`Stuck`-until-approved contract, not a port of `burlerengine`.
This is the second data point (after `loom`'s own review producers) for whether `internal/treadleengine` is ever fully retired — see the shipped `Retire perch` item's own note that its retirement is a separate call, made once `Tenter` lands.

## `Hardener` — the campaign

The operator's role in the hand-run campaign was mostly **gating** — approve, ask for another round — not irreplaceable judgment.
That is front-loadable into the seed instructions ("run until the gates are green or K rounds;
do not ask").
So `Hardener` can run **autonomously, overnight**, with reed + Go handling **auto-compaction** (which, per the insight above, *is* per-round respawn).
Model rotation across rounds (Opus / Fable / Sonnet) stays as a cheap diversity lens — convergence across *different* models is stronger evidence than N passes from one.

`Hardener`'s own worktree-spawn (via `fabric`) and safe-merge-back-to-parent lifecycle is `Shed`'s job (see `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation) — the same `loom`-shared lifecycle described above, with Hardener's own Preflight (below) instead of loom's.

### The sandbox dependency

`Hardener` cannot run against the module's own repo alone — it needs a **live sandbox repo** to do destructive, stateful things (create worktrees, junctions, spawn tmux, tear down) without corrupting the real repo,
and a maintained **live-driving suite** (`tools/sandbox/SANDBOX-<MODULE>-SUITE.md`) as the substrate-exercising vehicle.
Consequences carried from the hand-run method:

- **Deploy-first.**
  The suite runs the **deployed** binary, not the working tree — re-deploy after every source change or you validate a stale binary.
- **The decisive gate is N× concurrent smoke, not a quiet serial pass** — concurrency + CPU saturation is the amplifier that surfaces teardown races and leaked substrate state.
- **Zero stray substrate state at teardown** is itself an invariant under test.
- **Grow the suite with the module** — a bug found live leaves behind both a `//go:build smoke` regression test and, where visual, a suite scenario.

## The likely `lyx` shape (open)

`Tenter`'s defining trait — an accumulating, targeting review-loop — is precisely what lyx's thesis otherwise *replaces* with Go.
So this probably is **not** "Go takes over the orchestrator."
More likely: **lyx provides the deterministic scaffolding** and the **orchestrator brain stays an LLM** —

- **Go / lyx owns** (split across `Shed` and `Treadle`): provision/reset the sandbox, deploy the binary, run the slow gates (smoke suite, zero-stray-state), collect + structure results, maintain handoff files (via `internal/state`), the per-round respawn loop, teardown.
- **LLM orch-brain owns** (Tenter's judge, within `Treadle`): read results, accumulate understanding, decide what to target next, write the next round's focused prompt.
- **`burler`-shaped round agent** (see the `internal/burlerengine` package documentation): the A→B worker, spawned per round (drives the sandbox;
  `fix-scope: source`;
  commit-per-fix).

Whether the round agent literally imports the `burler` package or only follows the same `review-prompt-template.md` discipline is an implementation choice for when this is built.

## Dependencies (tentative)

- `internal/treadleengine` package documentation — the generic round-loop engine `Tenter` would configure (as-built;
  module doc deleted per the documentation lifecycle), independent of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` ever get built.
- `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation — the generic outer phase-FSM `Hardener` configures;
  same independence as above.
- `shuttle` — spawns the round agents and judges `Treadle`/`Tenter` drive.
- `internal/stencil` — fills the round-agent / orchestrator prompt templates (shared with `burler` and the review gate).
- `internal/state` — handoff + round artifacts on disk (the memory that makes respawn work).
- a **sandbox repo + live suite** — a provisioned environment and a maintained asset, not just code.
- `reed` transitively, via shuttle;
  possibly directly for the overnight/autonomous session + auto-compaction.

## Status / open questions

- ~~Persistent thread vs. per-round respawn~~ — resolved: per-round respawn via `Treadle`'s three-step loop (pre-round `progress-judge` → reviewer → post-round `progress-judge`);
  see above.
- ~~Naming: one module or two?~~ — resolved: `Tenter` (review-loop) + `Hardener` (`Shed` + `Tenter`, the campaign);
  see "Naming" above.
- The shared engine designs (round-runner interface, handoff/ledger format, pre-round-targeting mechanics for `Treadle`;
  the outer FSM for `Shed`) live in their own docs — not decided here, independently of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` themselves ever get scheduled.
- Exactly what the handoff must carry losslessly (key-ledger confirmed;
  what else?).
- The Go-scaffolding / LLM-brain boundary above.
- Whether it reuses the `burler` package or just the prompt template.
- Sandbox provisioning: how much lyx automates vs. a pre-existing sandbox repo.

**This module is post-loom and on-demand;
nothing here blocks the `burler → shed → loom` spine, nor the `Treadle`/`Shed` work, which proceeds independently of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` are ever scheduled.**

entries.title: A batchifier that groups small related cards into one Webster batch
entries.brief: A Go batchifier that sizes each card, runs large cards alone and groups small ones sharing files within a budget; several named profiles in batcher.yaml
entries.body:
## Why

`internal/batcher` has a registry but only the `identity` batchifier, so every card is its own Webster batch.
On `test-suite-change-amplification` (45 cards, 2026-10-03) each batch carried a fixed overhead besides the fork's own work: `record-batch`, `begin-batch`, three short Merriam turns and the fork's start-up, about 16–18 s per batch after quarry v0.2.1 (over a minute before it, #345), plus a fork prompt and Merriam polling per batch.
Many cards there take 40–120 s of work, so for them the overhead is a large share.

## Want

A mechanical batchifier (operator): it groups cards from the plan's own card fields (`Create`, `Edit`, `Uses`, renames), never from an LLM's judgment, selected through `batcher.yaml`'s `active` key, the identity batchifier staying the default.
Cards whose fields show no dependency on each other and no shared target can share a fork; a card that `Uses` another's `Create` follows it.

## Waits on `plan-glyph-precision`

Plans list file paths, not member glyphs, so card fields today only support file-level grouping, which is too coarse to be the point.
The batchifier is built once cards name the members they touch.

## Trade-offs to settle

- A larger batch gives the fork a larger context and makes a failure harder to localize to one card.
- The per-batch validation and drift check (`begin-batch`, `record-batch`) then runs per group, not per card; the operator wants plan drift caught as it happens.
- It should fit the parallel-execution direction in `manifest/designs/webster-parallel-execution.md`, where the same DAG decides which groups may run concurrently.

Member-level grouping depends on `plan-glyph-precision`; the quick fix below does not.

## Quick fix for tokens (operator, 2026-10-07)

The operator wants better batches now, as a quick fix for token use, not one batch per card, and chose it as the first token saving to build.
A token count over the five latest runs (`tools/tokencount`, 2026-10-07) put Webster's implementer forks at about 54% of all weighted tokens, nearly all of it cache reads: each fork reads a large context afresh (574M cache-read tokens over 81 forks; the two test-suite prunes ran 26 and 18).
For tokens, file-level grouping is enough: cards that edit the same files or package and follow each other in plan order share one fork, so their shared context is read once, with a cap on cards per batch to keep the context and failure localisation in bounds.
So this quick fix does not wait on `plan-glyph-precision`; finer member-level grouping can follow once cards name members.

A fork's size is not the master's cost: in the tests while Webster was built and hardened, a fork that succeeded added only about 1,000 tokens to the master (operator, 2026-10-07).
The cost is in the forks themselves: a sample of five forks on `bugfix-webster` started at 56–89K context tokens and grew to 155–217K over 80–140 messages, each message reading the whole context again.
Fewer forks with better batches means less repeated exploration and far fewer fork start-ups, so this is where the token saving starts.

## Design so far (operator, 2026-10-07)

A Go batchifier, never an LLM agent.
It cannot merge cards blindly: on 2026-10-07 single cards cost a Webster fork hundreds of thousands of tokens, and such a card must never share a fork.

- **Size each card mechanically**, from what the card and the disk say before the run: how many files it creates, edits or deletes, the line count of the files it edits, its test files and their size, and its `Uses` entries. A fork spends its tokens reading files and running tests, so these are the signals.
- **A card above a size threshold always runs alone.**
- **Small cards group** only when they follow each other in plan order (so no dependency is broken), share files or a package (so the shared context is read once), and stay within a size budget and a cap on cards per batch.
- **Calibrate** the estimate against real use: `tools/tokencount` extended to report tokens per fork, one fork being one Webster batch, compared with each batch's estimate to tune the weights. Start cautious, with a low budget and a cap of three or four cards.

## Deciding a batch from a cost model (proposed by the hub, accepted by the operator, 2026-10-07)

Grouping cards that merely follow each other and belong together is a start, not the rule (operator).
The batchifier decides from an estimated cost instead:

- **Cost model.** A fork costs roughly its messages times its context size, since every message reads the whole context again.
  Each card gets an estimate of its messages and of how much context it adds, from the signals above.
  Running card B in card A's fork saves B's fork start-up and the files they share, which are read once; it costs B carrying A's accumulated context in every message.
  So merging pays only when the cards share much and both are small, and the model, not a judgment, says when.
- **Overlap** is measured between the cards' read sets: the files they edit or use, their package and their test package.
  Two cards editing the same file share more than two cards in the same package.
- **Hard limits** hold whatever the model says: plan order and dependencies are never broken, a card above the threshold runs alone, and a batch stays within its card cap and budget.
- **Optimal split.** Plan order is a valid order, so the batchifier splits the card sequence into contiguous segments with the lowest total estimated cost: a small dynamic program over segments, exact and testable, rather than greedy merging.
  Moving cards next to each other where the dependencies allow, so cards of one package separated by an unrelated card can join, is a later step.

## Testing

- **The batchifier itself** is a pure function from cards and file stats to batches, so unit tests pin the hard limits on every input: order and dependencies kept, an oversized card alone, caps and budget kept.
- **The estimator offline**: past runs ran the identity batchifier, one fork per card, so `tools/tokencount` extended to tokens per fork gives a measured cost for every past card.
  Running the estimator on those plans and comparing with the measured cost calibrates the weights without running anything new.
- **The saving itself** cannot be measured offline, since a merged batch's cost was never observed.
  It is measured on real runs, switching profiles in `batcher.yaml` and comparing tokens per card against the identity profile's history, starting cautious.

## First step: calibration against past plans (operator, 2026-10-07)

The first cards of this task build the calibration, before any grouping:

- **Tokens per fork, tied to its card.** `tools/tokencount` reports each Webster fork's usage, and ties the fork to the card it ran, through the card name in the fork's prompt or the `begin-batch` and `record-batch` commits' times.
- **The past plans.** Every past run's plan is in the weft history (the `loom: plan artifacts for <slug>` commits), with the cards' `Create`, `Edit` and `Uses`.
- **The disk as it was.** File and test sizes come from the run's base commit on main, not today's tree.
- **The comparison.** The estimator runs on each past plan and its estimate per card is set against the card's measured tokens, to tune the weights before a profile groups anything.

`tools/` follows PATTERN.md and the repository's enforcement scans like every other package.

## Profiles in `batcher.yaml`

Several named batchifier profiles, all configured in `batcher.yaml`, with `active` naming the one in use, so the operator switches between them by changing one key (operator, 2026-10-07).
Not a single batchifier with one setting: each profile carries its own threshold, budget, card cap and weights, and the identity batchifier (one card, one batch) stays available as a profile of its own.

## Why

The operator works long-term on a branch of their own in its own worktree, not on `main`, which in a large project is not theirs to drive; that worktree is where they want their orch.

## Want

- `lyx orch` and `lyx batten` run from any drivable worktree in the hub, which then acts as that orch's home: pairs branch from its branch and land into it, and orch's scratch, handoffs and reed strand live in that worktree.
- More than one orch per hub, one per home worktree, without stepping on each other's pairs, board claims or reed sessions.

## Open points

- What "prime only" protects today and whether any of it must stay prime-bound (board writes, deploy, `lyx board prune`, the hub workspace).
- How a home worktree's branch reaches `main` (the operator's own merge, or a landing verb), and whether the board is per hub or per home.

entries.title: semantic-index: find code by concept, not by literal keyword
entries.brief: Semantic search over docstrings and comments; doubtful today, since agents now navigate well with grep
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday, kept by the operator on 2026-10-03 as someday.
Idea: semantic search over docstrings and comments (catalysts, embeddings, temporal decay), to find code by concept rather than literal keyword.
Operator: millhouse's codeguide (Claude-written `.md` navigation files, designed about six months earlier) gave a large exploration speedup then, but not any more, since Claude now searches well with grep; so the value of this is uncertain.
The design is under `## Design`.

## Design

> **Status: Speculative, not scoped.** Inspired by [Enzyme](https://www.enzyme.garden/blog/an-lsp-for-your-notes), a semantic search system for personal note vaults. This is the "deferred idea" [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry)'s own design proposal referred to ("a semantic/conceptual index... a separate, further-out idea, not part of this proposal") and the relationship-table row from the original quarry proposal ("have we written something conceptually similar, without shared vocabulary? — embeddings + temporal-decay weighting; not part of this proposal") — now named, not yet designed in depth. Per the documentation lifecycle, if this is ever picked up the durable parts fold into the owning package's doc when it lands; if abandoned, this file is simply deleted.

## The problem this responds to

Grep/text-search finds literal keyword matches.
It cannot answer "find code that does X" when the code implementing X uses none of the words a caller would naturally search for — e.g. "show me the error-handling patterns in this codebase" when error handling is spelled out in prose inside docstrings and comments but never literally contains the word "error" everywhere it matters. `quarry` (see [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry)) doesn't solve this either — it answers "what exactly references/defines this symbol," a precise, compiler-derived question, not "what have we conceptually written that's similar to this."

## Core mechanism, adapted from Enzyme

Enzyme indexes a personal notes vault;
the same shape maps onto a codebase's descriptive text (docstrings, comments, package `doc.go` headers):

1. **Catalyst generation.**
   Enzyme derives "thematic questions" from actual content per tag/link/ folder in a notes vault.
   For code, the analogous unit is likely per-package or per-module: derive thematic questions from that package's docstrings, comments, and `doc.go` header.
2. **Vector embedding.**
   Catalysts are embedded as vectors, with cosine similarity precomputed against every text chunk (docstring, comment block, doc header).
3. **Temporal decay weighting.**
   Recently written/modified text influences the index more heavily than old, rarely-touched text — the index shifts with the codebase's current shape, not a static snapshot taken once.
   For code specifically, "recency" is naturally available from git history (`git log` per file/function) — plausibly the same kind of SHA-diffing `internal/gitrepo` already does for other consumers, rather than a new mechanism.
4. **Semantic retrieval.**
   An agent searches catalyst vectors instead of guessing grep terms, surfacing conceptually related code across files/packages that share no literal vocabulary.

## Relationship to `quarry` and `raddle` — complementary, not overlapping

Same three-way split the original quarry proposal drew, now with a name for the third row:

| Module | Answers | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| `quarry` | "What exactly references/defines this symbol, right now?" | Deterministic, compiler-derived (LSP) |
| `raddle` | "Where does this conceptually belong, and why?" | LLM-authored/maintained narrative docs |
| `semantic-index` (this) | "Have we written something conceptually similar, without shared vocabulary?" | Embeddings + temporal-decay weighting |

None of these three replace either of the others — different question, different mechanism.

## Open questions (genuinely unscoped)

- **Indexing granularity.**
  Per-function docstring, per-file, or per-package `doc.go` — Enzyme's own granularity (tag/link/folder) doesn't map onto code 1:1;
  needs its own design pass.
- **Embedding provider.**
  Self-hosted vs. API-based — cost, latency, and offline/air-gapped operation all matter differently here than for a personal notes tool.
- **Temporal decay source.**
  Whether it reuses `gitrepo`'s `ChangedFilesSince`/SHA machinery directly, or needs its own recency signal.
- **Standalone vs. baked into loomyard.**
  Same question asked of `quarry` and `raddle` — lean build-inside-first, extract only once a second concrete consumer exists.
- **Consumer.**
  Presumably the planner (finding existing similar implementations before writing a card) and webster forks (finding a pattern to follow) — not yet concretely designed.

## Related

- [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry) — the precise, compiler-derived sibling;
  quarry's own design proposal named this as an out-of-scope, deferred idea.
- raddle.md — the curated-narrative sibling.
- `internal/gitrepo` — plausible source of the temporal-decay recency signal.
