entries.title: Bugfix: fabric and config propagation
entries.brief: Bugfix only: a weft without .weft/ drops LYX_PARENT, task config changes never reach the parent, and fabric ignores existing origin branches when it builds a pair
entries.body:
Bugfix only (operator, 2026-10-06): fix what each section below reports, with a regression test per fix that drives the real CLI wiring, not only fakes.
No new verbs, config keys or features; a reviewer treats any extension as a scope finding.
The board adds more bug sections here until the task starts.
One exception, by operator decision (2026-10-06): `fabric-add-adopt-remote` below is in scope whole, including `lyx fabric add` adopting existing origin branches.

## weft-lock-dir-drops-parent

### Bug

A strand launched in a pair whose weft worktree lacks the untracked `.weft/` lock directory gets no `LYX_PARENT`, silently.
`hubgeom.ResolveParent` reads the pair's origin record through `fabricengine.ReadOriginFor`, which requires both `_lyx/fabric/origin.json` and `.weft/`, and answers "no record" when either is missing.
`ResolveParent` then returns no parent, `hubgeom.reedGeometry` exports none, and nothing warns.

### Seen 2026-10-05

After moving `loom-bouncer-rounds` from another machine, its weft worktree was recreated by `lyx fabric reconcile` from the existing branch, which does not create `.weft/` (`lyx fabric add` does).
The driver, launched at 15:36:00, had no `LYX_PARENT`; `.weft/` appeared at 15:36:19 with the first weft write, and the Burler launched at 15:58 carries `LYX_PARENT='ly:orch'`.
The driver therefore could not reach its parent orchestrator.

### Fix

- Every path that creates or recreates a weft worktree creates `.weft/` (`reconcile`'s `weft_recreated` path at least).
- A present origin record with a missing lock directory is an error or a warning naming the gap, never a silent "no parent".

## config-reaches-parent

Seen 2026-10-04 twice: `pattern-init` first planned to keep PATTERN under `_lyx/` and needed a landing carry (dropped by moving PATTERN to warp), and `board-model`'s parent review found its D13 label list written into the pair's `_lyx/config/board.yaml`, which never reaches the parent.
Live config lives in weft, and a task's weft branch dies at landing, so any config change a task makes is lost unless the hub re-applies it by hand on main's weft.
Idea: either a landing step that carries `_lyx/config/` changes into the parent's weft (with a conflict stop), or task-made config changes declared in the PR description and applied by the hub as a checked step.

## fabric-add-adopt-remote

### Problem

Moving a running task to another machine needs a pair built from the task's existing warp and weft branches on origin.
Fabric handles an existing warp: `lyx fabric reconcile` adopts a warp worktree created outside lyx.
Finding the existing weft is the gap: `reconcile`, `checkout` and `add` probe only the local `refs/heads/<slug>-weft` (`weftBranchExists`).
When that ref is absent, `reconcile` forks a fresh dormant weft from the weft HEAD (`createDormantWeftForRawWarp`) and never looks at `origin/<slug>-weft`, so the run records and status are silently lost and the next push collides with origin.
Only `clone` adopts a weft branch from origin, and only for the prime.

### Workaround used on 2026-10-05

```
git -C <hub>/<repo>-weft branch --track <slug>-weft origin/<slug>-weft
git worktree add --track -b <slug> ../<slug> origin/<slug>
lyx fabric reconcile
```

With the local tracking weft branch in place, `reconcile` takes its `weft_recreated` path and wires junctions, portal and launchers.
`lyx batten run <slug>` from prime then resumed both the outer and the inner run, and the inner loom run continued from its producer row with a fresh agent.

The adopted pair's strands also lost their parent until the first weft write: see `weft-lock-dir-drops-parent` above.

### Proposal

When a branch exists on origin, fabric fetches it and checks it out as a tracking branch; it never creates a new local branch in its place.
`lyx fabric add <slug>` fetches `origin/<slug>` and `origin/<slug>-weft` when they exist, instead of refusing the warp branch as a diverged leftover.
Every other path that resolves a pair's weft branch (`reconcile`, `checkout`) checks `origin/<slug>-weft` the same way before forking a new one, as `clone` does.

entries.title: Shortcut commands built into lyx from one committed file
entries.brief: An embedded shortcut file, git-alias style: attach for reed attach, and one shortcut that starts the orch and attaches in the prime
entries.body:
Idea (operator, 2026-10-06): top-level shortcuts for the lyx commands the operator types most, declared in one simple file in this repo rather than as Go commands.

Examples:

- `attach` expands to `reed attach`.
- One shortcut for the prime runs `orch start`, then `reed attach`; the orch always runs in the prime.
  Name open: `spawn` was floated; `up` would read like `reed up`.
  It fits the decision recorded in task `bugfix-sessions` that start verbs never attach: the shortcut is where both happen, by naming `reed attach` explicitly.

## Shape (operator, 2026-10-06)

- The shortcuts are part of the deployed `lyx` binary, the same on every hub and repo: a committed file in the loomyard repo, embedded at build time (`go:embed`), never runtime config.
  No hub, repo or user can add or change one; changing a shortcut is a commit here and a deploy.
- The file maps a shortcut name to one lyx argv, or to a list of argvs run in order that stops at the first failure.
  Only lyx commands, never a shell string.
- At root construction lyx adds one cobra command per shortcut, in its own help group, whose `Short` names the expansion; running it re-dispatches the expanded args through the same root, so flags, envelopes and exit codes are the real command's.
  Extra args after the shortcut append to the last argv.
- A test fails when a shortcut names an existing command or another shortcut, or expands to a command that does not exist, so a broken file never builds into a binary that passes CI.

## Open

- Whether a shortcut may carry flags of its own or only append args.

More shortcuts get added here as the operator notices them.
Related notes: `ide-prime-setup` (a VS Code task that starts the orch) and `ide-reopen-prime` (reopen the prime window with one command).

entries.title: Spawned agents edit files with scripts; the no-script rule never reaches them
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-06 in `test-suite-prune-core`, batch 10's recovery strand: the agent edited `internal/websterengine/beginbatch_test.go` with an inline `python3 - <<'EOF'` script, and the edit left an unused `strconv` import that vet caught.

The rule "change files only with Edit or Write, never with a script that rewrites them (sed, awk, perl, python, node)" lives in `scribe:conversation`, a chat skill.
Spawned implementer, recovery and fixer roles load `scribe:prose`, `scribe:code-quality` and `scribe:testing`, so they never see it.

Fix direction: state the rule where every file-editing role reads it: the implementer and recovery stencils under `contracts/stencils/webster/`, the Burler fixer and Rework stencils, or one shared prefix they all compose.

entries.title: Run tabs overflow a narrow terminal once several runs are open
entries.brief: The status line row of run tabs prints full session names, so with five runs the rightmost fall off a narrow terminal unseen
entries.body:
## Seen 2026-10-06

With five runs and the prime open, the session row of the status line (the run tabs from `reed-status-tabs`) is wider than a narrow terminal, and the rightmost runs fall off the edge with no sign that they exist.
The row prints every session's full name with padding, and run slugs such as `test-suite-prune-core` are long.

## Options

1. Current session full, others truncated, overflow scrolls (recommended): the session the client is in shows its full name, every other session is cut to about 12 characters (`#{=12:session_name}`), and the row uses tmux's list mode (`list=on`, `list=focus`, left and right markers), so a row that still overflows scrolls with `<` and `>` markers and keeps the current session visible.
2. Index only for other sessions, the current one by full name: the most compact, but the operator has to remember which number is which run.
3. List-mode scrolling alone, full names kept: the least change, with the fewest sessions visible at once.
4. Wrap the session row onto further status lines: costs terminal height, and tmux has no automatic wrap, so reed would compute the split itself.

The run tabs' design is in the note `reed-status-tabs`.

entries.title: board: refuse scope edits to a running task
entries.brief: The board already marks running tasks; a write that changes the scope of a running task is refused
entries.body:
A task whose run has started can still be edited on the board.
On 2026-10-06 the orch folded two new issues into `bugfix-sessions` with `lyx board intake import --into` while that run sat planned and parked before Webster, so the board entry no longer matched the plan its run was executing.

The status already exists and is stored on the entry: the loom run writes `status` on every transition (`SetBoardStatus` in `internal/loomcli/wiring.go`, through `boardStatus`), such as `running · Webster`, and landing sets `done`; `lyx board list --text` shows it.
Nothing refuses a write to an entry whose status is set.
The operator wants the lock to start when a task is claimed (operator, 2026-10-06): the status is set at once when its run starts, before Discussion, so no edit slips in between the start and the first transition.

Wanted (operator, 2026-10-06): a write that changes a running task's scope (body, brief, issues, labels, a merge or an intake `into`) is refused with the reason, naming the run.
New findings go to a note of their own instead.

entries.title: Recovery prompt gives no guidance on uncommitted changes left by the prior attempt
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #406](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/406).

A recovery run for a Webster task segment was started with the reason `none` and an instruction to continue from the committed tree.
The worktree nevertheless held a large uncommitted body of work from the earlier attempt (dozens of files, thousands of changed lines).
The recovery prompt did not mention these changes or say whether to trust and keep them or to discard them, so the agent had to judge on its own whether the earlier work was sound.

This is abnormal because the recovery prompt contradicts the worktree state: "continue from the committed tree" is not true when the tree is dirty.
The agent kept the work only after verifying it independently (build, both test tiers, a fresh rerun of the segment's check).

Suggested fix: when lyx starts a recovery, have it detect uncommitted changes in the worktree and name them in the recovery prompt, together with an explicit keep-or-discard instruction.

Provenance: task `test-suite-prune-core`; note `10-websterengine-prune-recovery.md`.

entries.title: Open an extra named agent strand through shuttle
entries.brief: Open a named Claude session in a strand with no task, through shuttle, so it keeps its name; for extra strands in the prime
entries.body:
The operator wants extra Claude strands beside the orch in the prime, such as one for exploring the repo, added by the orch on request (operator, 2026-10-06).

Tried 2026-10-06: `lyx reed add --name explore --cmd claude` runs a bare `claude`, so the pane title is `ly:explore` but the Claude session gets no `--name`, and reed records no session id, so the watchdog's session-name repair (`internal/reedengine/namerepair.go`) skips it.

Every agent in lyx runs through shuttle (operator), so this needs a shuttle engine extension: open a named LLM session in a strand with no turn and no prompt, started with the strand name and its session id recorded, so the watchdog keeps the name across a compact.
The verb that calls it sits above shuttle, which has no CLI of its own (see the `creel` note), and not in reed, which shuttle depends on.

Open: where such a strand goes in the reed layout relative to the orch, and how several share the space.

entries.title: An operator decision can amend the card of a begun Webster batch
entries.brief: rebaseline refuses begun cards and reset needs a fresh run loom cannot start, so a mid-run decision never reaches the plan
entries.body:
An operator decision made while Webster runs cannot reach the plan card of a batch that has begun.
Seen 2026-10-07 in `bugfix-sessions`: the operator decided that the submit settle of card 1 comes from config, while batch 1 was running.
The decision went into the decision record, but `lyx webster rebaseline --card 01` refused ("the edited plan changes the cards of a batch this run already begun"), and its way forward, `lyx webster reset --to start` then `lyx webster run --fresh`, has no path through loom: the Webster producer always runs with `Fresh: false` (`internal/shedadapters/webster.go`).
An edit left on disk while the master recorded the batch blocked the run with `plan_drifted` until the plan was restored.
So the card still says "hard-coded constant" while the code reads config, and the Webster review sees a deviation the operator approved.

Wanted (operator, 2026-10-07): an operator decision taken mid-Webster lands in the plan and the decision record together, without extra review or PR-Gate steps, whether or not the card's batch has begun.

Since `bugfix-webster` (d536a1a4e) the drift advice offers rebaseline only for an edit that keeps begun batches' cards, and rebaseline accepts an edit to a failed, dead or stuck batch.
Still open: a decision against a begun, non-terminal batch, and the Webster producer's `Fresh: false`.


## From issue #413

Imported from [issue #413](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/413).

## What happened

A loom run was sent back to `Plan-Write` by a `goto` after the `Batchifier` had already handed batch 1 to `Webster` and the batch's card had been begun.
`Plan-Write`, `Plan-Bouncer`, `Plan-Burler` and `Batchifier` then completed again with an edited plan, and the run reached `Webster` again.
`lyx webster record-batch 1` refused with `plan_drifted`:

```
webster: on-disk plan fingerprint does not match this run's recorded state: ...; the plan changed since state.json was created; way forward: run `lyx webster rebaseline --card 01` to accept the edit, or restore the plan the run recorded with "lyx webster restore-plan", otherwise 1) lyx webster reset --to start; 2) lyx webster run --fresh
```

`lyx webster rebaseline --card=1` then refused as well:

```
webster: the edited plan changes the cards of a batch this run already begun: batch 1 card 01-paced-text-submit changed since it was begun; way forward: restore those cards in the plan, or 1) lyx webster reset --to start; 2) lyx webster run --fresh
```

The loom halted `blocked` at `Webster` with anomaly `escalation-to-human`.

## Why this is abnormal

- The loom recipe itself re-ran the plan stages after Webster state existed, so the drift was produced by lyx's own flow, not by a stray manual edit.
- The first refusal names `rebaseline` as the way forward, but for a plan that edits an already-begun card `rebaseline` can never succeed.
  The first refusal's advice leads straight into the second refusal.
- The only exits left are `lyx webster reset --to start` and `lyx webster run --fresh`, which discard the run's Webster progress.
  Nothing in the first refusal says that the rebaseline path is closed for this case.

## What to do

- Make the loom `goto` back to `Plan-Write` reset or rebaseline Webster state as part of the loop-back when batches were already begun, or refuse the `goto` with a clear reason.
- Have `lyx webster record-batch` check whether `rebaseline` would be accepted and only offer it as a way forward when it would; otherwise name the reset path first.

Provenance: task `bugfix-sessions`; notes `loom-halt.md`, `webster-refusal-record-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-rebaseline.md`.

Correction to issue #413 (orch, 2026-10-07): the reflection read the drift as produced by the goto to Plan-Write; the drift came from the orch's hand edit of card 1 while batch 1 was recorded, and the goto had happened before this Webster run began.
Its finding stands: `record-batch` offers `rebaseline` as the way forward for a begun card, where `rebaseline` always refuses, so the advice should name only paths that can succeed.


#416 (a stale report after a Plan-Write goto) is fixed in `bugfix-webster` (d536a1a4e): begin-batch archives a report with no batch record.

entries.title: Who in a running task receives an instruction
entries.brief: Driver forwarding, an alias for the active strand kept by loom, or an on-call LLM per run: open for a brainstorm
entries.body:
Who in a running task receives an instruction from the orch or the operator, open for a brainstorm (operator, 2026-10-07).

Seen 2026-10-07: an operator decision about card 1 of `bugfix-sessions` arrived while Webster ran.
The orch has to know which agent owns the content at that moment (Discussion-Write, the plan agent, the Webster master, a Burler round) and message it, or fall back on a goto; mid-Webster no agent can change a begun card at all (`webster-amend-begun-card`).
The orch editing the run's files itself is never the answer.

Options raised:

- The driver forwards: it knows its current producer and the strand doing the work. One address per run, but an LLM relays in a turn of its own, may reword, and its stencil does not do this today.
- An alias such as `ly:<slug>:active` for the strand that owns the current step: deterministic, no LLM between.
  Creel must not know what runs or what is active (operator): it owns messages and injects only.
  So creel could at most store a plain name-to-name alias that loom itself sets at every producer transition, knowing nothing of its meaning; or the alias lives outside creel altogether.
- An on-call LLM per run, woken when an instruction needs judgment about the run (what a decision means for the plan, who must do what). The operator considered this before the driver existed, when the driver was a Go process; it rebuilds its context each time it wakes, and it adds a role.
- The driver itself becomes that on-call role, with read access to the plan: it already lives the whole run, but grows heavier than a step driver.

Plain routing ("deliver to whoever works now") and judgment ("what does this mean for the run") may want different answers.

Steps with no LLM at all: the Go producers (Preflight, Batchifier, the verify gates, Publish, Finalize, teardown) have no strand to deliver to.
A message could wait in its queue for the next LLM producer if the alias is resolved at delivery rather than at send, but that agent may not be the right one (after Batchifier comes the Webster master, while the instruction may concern the plan).
This suggests a split to discuss:
- Content ("the settle comes from config") goes into the decision record, which is durable, read by every later LLM producer, and needs no live receiver.
- Only an instruction that must act now needs a live receiver, and the most urgent one, stop, is a run pause (`lyx batten pause`), which works during a Go step too.

Operator leaning (2026-10-07): the driver takes the message.
It runs a Sonnet agent on purpose, to have judgment; it is the one LLM alive for the whole run, Go steps included, it knows where the run stands, and it receives messages while its `shed step` runs in the background.
With a message it could record content with `lyx loom decision add` (a lyx verb, not a source edit), forward it to the strand that owns the current step, or pause the run or ask for a goto.

Refined (operator, 2026-10-07): every instruction for a run is posted to its driver, which gets only the short reminder (sender and subject) and does not read the body by default.
Knowing which agent works now, it either reads it itself or forwards it with `lyx creel forward` (see the `creel` note), so the receiving agent talks to the original sender, not to the driver: a minimal routing job.

entries.title: A pane listing every gate of a run as a checklist with timings
entries.brief: Every gate of the run with a tick box and its elapsed time, in a pane of its own; an idea, not a priority
entries.body:
Idea, not a priority (operator, 2026-10-07): a full list of a run's gates, shown as a checklist with a tick box per gate and how long each ran or has run so far.
It holds too much for a status line or a pane border, so it likely needs a pane of its own in the run's reed session.

entries.title: A producer runs two live agents side by side
entries.brief: Shuttle starts and waits on two agents in one step and lets them talk; the base discussion-advisor and burler-split both need
entries.body:
A producer that runs two live agents side by side in one step, each in a strand of its own (operator, 2026-10-07).
Today every producer runs one agent through shuttle and waits on its one turn end; the Webster master's forks are sub-agents inside one session, not two strands.

Two notes need it:

- `discussion-advisor`: beside Discussion-Write, a second agent explores the task and the code and answers its design questions as they arise.
- `burler-split`: a review-only agent forking its lenses, and in parallel a stronger fixer that orients, then fixes and validates the findings.

What the shared capability has to cover: shuttle starting both agents with their own model-specs, waiting on both and knowing when each is done (the hard part, see `shuttle-crucible`), ending the step when the producer's own rule says so, and the two agents talking to each other directly, which points at `creel`.
Built once, it serves both notes.

Inside one producer, not two parallel shed producers (operator, 2026-10-07): shed is a linear machine, one current producer, one history, and pause, goto and routing each assume one step at a time.
Parallel producers would need fork and join in the recipe and rules for one branch halting while the other is done; inside one producer the two agents are invisible to shed, which sees one step with one outcome.

entries.title: Shuttle reads turns right: a Stop is always taken, a turn end without output holds
entries.brief: Wait misses a valid Stop (#411/#415); an asking turn end ends the run (#407); a replay corpus and live runs test turn reading; the post-Enter redraw wait in shuttle.yaml
entries.body:
## Goal

Shuttle reads Claude Code's turns right: a valid Stop is always taken, a turn end without output never ends a run, and a replay corpus proves both.
Split from the run-errors bundle (operator, 2026-10-07).

## Shuttle's wait never takes a valid Stop (#411, #415)

Seen 2026-10-06 in `test-suite-prune-rest` and 2026-10-07 in `bugfix-sessions`, both at a Webster-Burler round 2.

- The burler ended its turn: `events.jsonl` held a valid Stop past `promptOffset`, with `background_tasks: []`, and both output files existed.
- `lyx shed step` never returned and had no child process; the verify gate never ran.
- A SIGQUIT goroutine dump showed the step parked in the poll loop both times:

```
shuttleengine.(*Run).Wait            internal/shuttleengine/wait.go:305 (realClock.Sleep)
shuttleengine.(*Runner).RunGated     internal/shuttleengine/run.go:643
burlerengine.(*Engine).Run           internal/burlerengine/engine.go:197
shedadapters.(*BurlerProducer).Call  internal/shedadapters/burler.go:419
shedengine.(*Shed).stepLocked        internal/shedengine/run.go:232
```

So `pollEventsTick` (`wait.go:613`) kept not returning Done for a Stop that looks complete.

- Leads: the first burler's transcript ends with a `continued-in` entry pointing at a new session, so a session switch may move the events the wait reads; an output-file or offset check is the other suspect.
  In both cases the shuttle run started a fresh strand while a round-1 strand of the same role had been used before.
- Not a suspend: the system journal shows the first case wholly awake, and the second had four minutes awake after its Stop before a hibernate (08:39:12–09:56:11), which only explains the stall's length.
- Run dirs: `.lyx/shuttle/976daeeb219e18f87d1a6954c562b64e` (first), `.lyx/shuttle/d9a47c207a52c3c94532ffc39927988b` (second).
- Wanted: find why the wait does not return, and give it a bounded exit so no SIGQUIT is needed.
  The crash-resume path after a SIGQUIT worked as designed.
- A look-alike that is not this bug: on 2026-10-07 in `bugfix-webster` an idle burler pane with a step that did not move on was a verify gate running for over ten minutes; the dump showed `evaluateGate` → `verifyrun.run` → `exec.Cmd.Wait`.
  Task `run-recovery` makes the two tell apart without a dump.

## A turn end without output holds the run instead of ending it (#407)

A turn end without every output file present ends a shuttle run as `asking`, a terminal outcome, while the agent stays alive in its pane.
Nothing waits on that agent any more: an answer sent into its session makes it work on unobserved, and resuming the producer starts a second agent on the same outputs.
Seen 2026-10-06 in `bugfix-sessions` Plan-Write: the plan agent asked, ly:orch answered in the session, the driver resumed, and shuttle spawned `plan-2` beside the still-working first agent.
The same rule makes any message to a working agent dangerous: it replies, its turn ends without outputs, and the run halts as `asking`.

- A turn end with every output file present is done, as today; a dead agent and a timeout end the run, as today.
- A turn end without the outputs holds the run with the agent alive: shuttle notifies the parent once and keeps waiting on the same agent.
- An answer to the agent is a new turn in the same session; shuttle keeps waiting.
- Resuming the producer attaches to the held run instead of starting a new agent.
- Every message to a working agent carries a fixed tail, "Answer briefly, then continue your task"; senders add it today, and `creel` adds it once it lands.

The cost: a stop no longer halts the run at once; the parent's notice and the run's timeout are the only signals.
`bugfix-sessions` (#400) already removes a live agent of the same outputs before a fresh run, which ends the duplicate but not the lost answer.

The background-shell half of #407: a turn end judged while a shell Master started still ran past `background_shell_wait_min` risks a premature stuck verdict; lyx keeps waiting on the shell or reports its final state rather than noting it may still run.

## The post-Enter redraw wait comes from `shuttle.yaml`

`submitRedrawSettle` in `internal/claudeengine/session.go`, the wait after Enter before the input box is read again, is a hardcoded 300 ms.
It comes from `shuttle.yaml` beside `submit_settle_ms`, read through `claudeengine.NewFromConfig`.

## Replay corpus and live runs

Harden shuttle against how Claude Code behaves in practice, found by running it, rather than one fix per misread found in a live run (operator, 2026-10-06).

Seen on 2026-10-06 alone: false "asking" stops at Plan-Write (twice, one spawning a second plan agent) and on a Webster master whose fork was still measuring (#407), a fork killed by an API error recorded as `dead_reason: asking`, and a burler turn end never taken at all (#411).
Each came from behaviour shuttle had not been written for: forks and background shells outliving a turn, messages arriving mid-run, skill loads, a session `continued-in` another, API errors.
Shuttle reads undocumented Claude Code internals (transcript line shapes, `custom-title`), which change between Claude Code versions.

Two parts:

- A replay corpus: every misread from a real run is saved as a fixture (the transcript and shuttle's events, with what happened), and shuttle's classification is tested against the whole corpus. Cheap and deterministic; today's cases are the first fixtures.
- Live runs: real Claude sessions driven through scripted scenarios that provoke the hard cases (long background shells, forks, a message mid-turn, skill loads, a compact, an interrupt, a question), checking shuttle's reading against the known answer. Costs tokens; catches a Claude Code release that changes behaviour before a task run meets it.

Starting point (operator, 2026-10-06): loomyard has no crucible of its own yet.
The repo's `crucible/` holds the hand-run review-and-fix loop that hardened reed, written for millhouse (`_mill/` paths, round-agent profiles copied into `.claude/agents/`), and the operator expects it can be rewritten for this more easily than starting over.
Its README names the behaviour-based form, running a live-substrate module in a sandbox, a `hardener` board note, which is no longer on the board.

What the crucible should settle is which signals tell the truth.
Shuttle already gets turn ends from Claude Code's official Stop hook, written into each run's `events.jsonl` with its `background_tasks`; the misreads come from treating "the turn ended" as "the work is done", and #411 is a Stop that arrived and was never taken.
Candidates to combine: the Notification hook Claude Code sends when it waits for input, a non-empty `background_tasks` meaning not done whatever the turn says, and quiet over time.
Codex, a planned second engine (`codex-engine`), has its own turn-complete hook with a different shape, so each engine needs its own hard cases behind shuttle's common outcomes.

entries.title: A run shows what it waits on and comes back up as it was
entries.brief: A running gate visible in status and on screen; no stray strands after a crash (#408/#409); batten run brings its child back; an orch resume verb that wakes the driver
entries.body:
## Goal

The operator and the orch can see what a run waits on, and a run comes back up as it was after a crash or a halt.
Split from the run-errors bundle (operator, 2026-10-07).

## A running verify gate is visible in status and on screen

After an agent ends its turn, a Go gate (`verifyrun`: build, unit, integration, smoke vet) can run for many minutes while the agent's pane sits idle; the operator and the orch read it as a hang (`orch-cycle-hardening` and `board-config-per-worktree` 2026-10-05, `bugfix-fabric` and `bugfix-webster` 2026-10-07, where the orch SIGQUIT-ed a gate it took for part 1).

- `lyx loom status` names the gate and how long it has run, such as `Webster-Burler: verify running 6m (go test -tags integration)`, for every producer.
  On 2026-10-07 `bugfix-sessions` showed `verify Webster-Burler gate (attempt 1, since 10:15)` in `waiting` while `bugfix-webster`, in the same producer, showed nothing: find which gate path skips it.
- On screen: shuttle owns the gate, so it sets a pane user option on the agent's strand when a gate starts (e.g. `@gate=verify`, `@gate_start=<time>`) and clears it when the gate ends; reed's status format shows it with the elapsed time computed at each refresh, such as `webster ⏳verify 2m14s` (operator, 2026-10-07).
- The same holds for every Go-side wait after an agent's turn: the Webster verify gate, the Burler round's verify, Publish's merge-in verify.

## reed: stray strands after a crash (#408, #409)

- **Bare claude above a dormant orch (#408).** The folder-open chain in `internal/vscode/config.go` runs `lyx reed add --if-absent --unless-name orch --name claude`; `--unless-name` skips only while the orch strand is live (`AddStrandUnless`, `internal/reedengine/strand.go`), so after a reboot a bare `claude` strand lands above the dormant orch.
  Expected: an orch strand, live or dormant, blocks the bare add; let `--unless-name` match a persisted dormant strand, or run `lyx reed resume` before the add.
- **Resume revives finished strands (#409).** After a crash, `lyx reed resume` in `test-suite-prune-core` recreated a burler whose round was done, beside the next producer's own strand.
  A strand stays in reed's state after its work is done, since only the shuttle wait that would remove it died with the crash.
  Expected: resume brings back only strands with work left, or a strand leaves reed's state as soon as its shuttle run reaches a final outcome.

## batten run brings its child back up

`lyx batten run <slug>` on a run whose batten process had died, with its inner loom run halted (paused, blocked or failed), started batten, which logged "inner shed run halted; waiting for the operator to resume it" and waited without bringing the loom run back up; the orch had to run `lyx loom start --no-attach` in the task worktree as a second step.
Seen 2026-10-07 restarting the three bugfix runs after their batten processes died; the runs went on only once their drivers were also messaged.

Wanted (operator, 2026-10-07): `batten run` brings its current producer, the loom run, back up as it was, driver included.
The loom run itself stays where it halted, since that halt is its own; resuming it remains a separate step (a resume, or a message to its driver).

## An orch resume verb

Seen 2026-10-06: the prime's reed window jumped to other sessions "by itself" while the operator watched the orch.
The cause was the orch's own `lyx loom start` calls in task worktrees: the orch runs inside reed's tmux, so `$TMUX` is set, and `lyx loom start` without `--no-attach` runs `tmux switch-client` onto the task's session (`internal/loomcli/start.go`), taking the operator's terminal with it.
`lyx orch start` does the same without `--no-attach` (`internal/orchcli/handover.go`).

The orch role (`contracts/stencils/orch/orch-template-role.md`) tells the orch to resume a halted child with `lyx loom start`, an operator verb whose job includes handing over the terminal.
In practice the call also did not move the runs: a live driver resumed only once the orch messaged it.

Direction:

- The orch resumes a child through a verb with no interactive side effect: a resume verb that only records the decision and wakes the run's driver (or batten), never spawning or attaching anything.
  The role stencil names that verb and never `lyx loom start`.

Start verbs no longer attach for any caller; attaching is only `lyx reed attach` (operator decision 2026-10-06, landed in `bugfix-sessions`, 26f329be7).
This note keeps the orch resume verb.


## From issue #420

Imported from [issue #420](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/420).

## What happened

A `lyx shed step` on a Burler round (Webster-Burler, round 3) never returned an envelope.
The round's agent finished, but the step stayed in the gated boundary for about 19 minutes until the operator's delegate sent SIGQUIT; the process exited with code 2.
The trace held `shed: step` and no `shed: step done`, and no `fabric: mutation` records.
The status afterwards was unchanged: `state: running`, `last_step.finished: false`, `interrupt_policy: reinvoke`.
The next `lyx loom step` then wrote a `loom-crash-resume` note for a suspected driver crash.

The goroutine dump shows the main goroutine blocked in a syscall wait on the child process, with the stack:

`verifyrun.run` -> `os/exec.(*Cmd).Wait` <- `verifytree.Verify` <- `loomshed.NewVerifyGate` <- `burlerengine.repairReportBeforeGate` <- `shuttleengine.(*Run).evaluateGate` <- `handleGatedBoundary` <- `Wait` <- `RunGated` <- `burlerengine.(*Engine).Run` <- `shedadapters.(*BurlerProducer).Call` <- `shedengine.(*Shed).Step`.

All other goroutines were idle, so nothing else was working: the step was waiting only on the verify command's `Cmd.Wait`.

## Why this is abnormal

The verify gate is meant to end in a pass or fail verdict.
`verifyrun.run` is passed a duration argument (a timeout), yet the wait outlived it by many minutes.
A likely cause is that the verify command's descendants keep the output pipes open, or the child is not killed on timeout, so `Cmd.Wait` does not return.
Which of those it was is not established by the dump.

## What to do

- Make the verify command's wait bounded: kill the whole process group on timeout and set `Cmd.WaitDelay` so `Wait` returns even when a grandchild holds the pipes.
- Treat a timed-out verify as a gate failure with a clear reason, not a silent hang.
- Consider a step-level watchdog that logs which gate the step is waiting in, so an operator can see the hang without a SIGQUIT dump.

Provenance: task `bugfix-webster`; notes `repair-20261007-webster-burler-r3-sigquit.md`, `loom-crash-resume.md`.

Correction (orch, 2026-10-07): the premise above does not hold.
`verifyrun.run`'s duration argument is `cmd.WaitDelay` (10 s), which only bounds the pipe read after the process exits (`internal/verifyrun/run.go`); nothing puts a deadline on the gate.
The dump caught a gate about 20 s old: `.lyx/verify/running.yaml` appeared at 10:33:37 and the SIGQUIT came at 10:34, while the burler's turn ended at 10:23.
The ten minutes before the gate were most likely shuttle's `background_shell_wait_min` (10) wait after the burler's turn end, with background agents showing in its pane.
So two things belong here: that wait is silent in status and on screen, looking the same as a hang or a gate, and a verify gate has no deadline.

entries.title: A task branch is always on the remote
entries.brief: Go pushes the warp branch wherever it pushes the weft; a loom status push survives a diverged remote (#418)
entries.body:
## Goal

Every task's work is on the remote at all times, and loom's pushes mid-run survive a moved remote.
Split from the run-errors bundle (operator, 2026-10-07).

## The warp branch is pushed with the weft

A task branch should be on the remote at all times (operator, 2026-10-06), so that a crash, a lost machine or a look from another machine never meets work that exists only locally.

Seen 2026-10-06 in `test-suite-prune-rest`: the warp branch was 19 commits ahead of `origin/test-suite-prune-rest` while its weft was in sync.
The last warp push was at 15:40 by Webster (`internal/websterengine/sequence.go` pushes after its batches); the eleven Webster-Burler fix commits from 19:11 on and a merge of main at 19:52 stayed local until Publish.

Cause: agents commit warp with their own `git commit`, and pushing is left to whichever loop owner happens to push.
A Burler round commits each fix and never pushes (`internal/burlerengine/doc.go`, `FixScopeSource`, and its prompt in `internal/burlerengine/prompt.go`).
`lyx fabric commit`, `push` and `sync` cover the weft only, so a weft push never carries the warp along.

Operator direction: the remote is never behind, and that must not rest on agents.
The operator first wanted every agent to commit through a `lyx fabric` verb that pushes warp with weft, then judged that agents will keep running `git commit` whatever their prompt says.
So the push belongs to Go: wherever the weft is pushed after a step, the warp branch is pushed with it, whatever made the commits.

## Loom status push can hit a diverged remote mid-run (#418)

Seen once in `bugfix-sessions` (drive report 20261006-121941): during Discussion-Burler round 1, loomcli logged `status push failed ... remote diverged`; the next transition pushed fine.
Distinct from #404 (Publish push).
A status push recovers from a diverged remote by itself rather than logging a failure.

entries.title: Orch compact cycle always times out before reload
entries.brief: tickCompacting reads a stale pre-compact turn end, so every compact cycle waits out the handoff timeout and reloads late
entries.body:
## What happens

A compact cycle never sees its own compaction finish, so it always waits out the handoff timeout and aborts.
Seen 2026-10-07 on the hub orch:

- 12:05:39 the watcher enters `compacting` and types `/compact`.
- 12:06:41 the compaction boundary is written to the transcript.
- 12:15:41 the phase ends with `last_abort_reason: "compaction timed out"`.
- The next idle turn end finds the boundary through the auto-compaction path (`CompactedSince`) and only then sends the reload, about ten minutes late.

## Cause

`tickCompacting` (`internal/orchengine/watcher.go`) decides the compaction landed from the context reading of `st.ReadingTurnEnd`.
That field is written only in the idle phase (the `st.Phase == PhaseIdle && isTurnEnd(ev)` branch of the tick's event read), never while the phase is `compacting`.
So it stays on the turn end from before `/compact`, whose reading can never show `Compacted`, and the turn ends after the compaction are not read.

## Side effects

- The cycle counts as aborted: `cycle_count` does not move and `last_deferral` is set, which can push back the next automatic cycle.
- A `distill` request queued during the cycle is removed as stale (`orch: stale cycle request removed`) instead of being acted on.

## Fix direction

In `compacting`, take each turn end read after the phase entry as the reading candidate, or ask the transcript for a boundary after `PhaseEnteredAt` directly, as the auto path does.
A test drives a compact cycle through a turn end that follows the boundary and asserts the reload starts without the timeout.

entries.title: One session-state model in shuttle that every module reads
entries.brief: Shuttle owns busy/idle-done/idle-stalled/asking/dead per agent as timestamped events; batten, the orch watcher, creel and reed stop guessing
entries.body:
Decided in direction by the operator 2026-10-07: unify how lyx knows what an agent session is doing, owned by shuttle.

## Why

Every module guesses an agent's state its own way, and each guess has failed:

- Batten judges a run quiet from the child's status file, which changes only at a step's end; on 2026-10-07 an API error stalled all five runs and the quiet notices came 45 min later, long after the agents were resumed by hand, naming no cause.
- The orch watcher runs its own idle probe and reads turn ends, and its compact cycle missed its own compaction (`orch-compact-timeout`).
- Shuttle's turn reading misses Stops and waits on finished background shells (#411, #420; `shuttle-turns`).
- An injected text races the operator's typing between the idle probe and the Enter (see `creel`).
- Nothing notices a live session stopped by an API error, machine sleep or a dropped network; elapsed time and transcript growth cannot tell it apart from a long simulation or test run.

## Direction

Shuttle owns one session-state model per agent strand, and batten, the orch watcher, creel and reed read it instead of inferring their own:

- `busy`: a turn is running, however long; a long tool call or simulation is never mistaken for a stall.
- `idle-done`: the turn ended with its output.
- `idle-stalled`: the session is idle but its step is not done, or the turn ended on an API error or an interrupt; detected in seconds from state, not from a timeout.
- `asking`: the agent waits on an answer.
- `dead`: the pane or process is gone.

Each state change is an event with a timestamp, so a consumer reacts to the change and keeps a history of changes only, never ticks (see `orch-notice-channel`).
`idle-stalled` gets a bounded resume: shuttle tells the session to continue, with a retry cap and backoff, then halts the run visibly with the cause.

## Sources, never guesses

Today's misreads all came from inference: scraping the pane (the idle probe, the paste race), scanning the transcript heuristically (missed `queued_command` lines, #411/#420), and judging from mtime or elapsed time (the 45 min quiet notice).
The model rests on what Claude Code itself reports:

- Hooks are the truth: `UserPromptSubmit` is a turn start, `Stop` a turn end (its payload carries `background_tasks`), `Notification` an agent asking or waiting on a permission. Shuttle already installs the Stop hook; the others are a few lines in the same hook config writing to the same event file. Hooks are only for agent sessions; lyx's own Go processes know their state already.
- An API error is a marked transcript entry; whether Claude Code also has a hook for it is to be checked.
- Liveness is the process: a dead pid is `dead`.
- The pane is a cross-check only, never the basis.
- Missing or contradicting signals give `unknown`, shown, never a silent guess.

Tests replay the real transcripts and hook payloads that today's and yesterday's failures left behind as fixtures.

## Built in small steps

A big-bang rewrite of shuttle is the risk; nothing changes behavior until it is proven:

1. `shuttle-turns` lands first.
2. Shadow mode: shuttle computes and logs the state beside today's guesses, with no consumer reading it; disagreements are read against real runs.
3. One consumer moves at a time, each its own small task: batten's quiet notice first (worst case a wrong notice), then the orch watcher, then creel.

## Relations

`shuttle-turns` fixes turn reading and is a first piece of this; this note is the step after it lands.
`run-recovery` covers dead processes; `orch-notice-channel` and `orch-compact-timeout` are consumers that would read this state; `creel` stage 2 delivers on it.

entries.title: Prime-side fabric push and sync publish unpushed main commits
entries.brief: Since run-pushes, lyx fabric push/sync in the prime (and lyx config) push main too, so unpushed hub commits skip the full test suite
entries.body:
Found at run-pushes' PR-Gate (PR #422), 2026-10-07; a deliberate design choice there (its Decision 5), not a defect.

In the prime, `lyx fabric push` and `sync` now push the parent branch (`main`) as well as the records side.
That includes the `sync` that `lyx config` runs after a change, which pushes whether or not the call made a commit.
So when the hub holds local `main` commits not yet pushed, a `lyx config --set` publishes them without the full `go test ./...` the hub runs before every push to `main`.

## Direction

Either gate the prime-side push of the parent branch (refuse, or push only the records side, when the parent branch has unpushed commits the call did not make), or keep the hub from ever holding unpushed local `main` commits.

entries.title: Plan checks let a card command reach the fabric repo
entries.brief: card-batching card 08 told its fork to run tokencount on ../card-batching-weft; neither validate-plan nor Plan-Review caught it, and Webster audit then wedged the run
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-07 in card-batching: card 08 (`_lyx/plan/08-calibrate-template.md:16`) ordered `go run ./tools/tokencount ... -history ../card-batching-weft`. The fork obeyed, record-batch failed the audit with `fabric-reference`, `recover-batch` refused `needs_fresh` and `accept-audit` refused too, leaving only a full `reset --to start`.

The plan validator should refuse a card command that names a path outside the tracked tree (the weft repo above all), so Plan-Review never passes one. Separately, a `fabric-reference` from a batch with no commit and HEAD unchanged cannot have touched the tree; `accept-audit` could accept it.
The no-commit case has since landed (`accept-audit --batch`, 83a7d6691).

Seen again 2026-10-07 in shuttle-turns, batch 13 (cards 13–16): a fork, most likely for `15-replay-corpus`, read other worktrees' shuttle events (`*/.lyx/shuttle/*/events.jsonl`, `*-weft/.lyx/shuttle/...`) with `cat`/`jq` to build a corpus, then committed all four cards.
The findings were read-only and pathless, but the batch had commits, so `accept-audit --batch` refused and the hub had to `git reset --keep` the batch's start and redo all four cards.
Two wants:

- `accept-audit --batch` accepts pathless `fabric-reference` findings on a batch with commits when the findings come from read-only commands, or the audit tells a read from a write in the first place.
- The plan stencil steers a corpus or fixture card to committed test data, never to live files of other worktrees.


## From issue #424

Imported from [issue #424](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/424).

## What happened

In one loom run, webster batch 08 failed `lyx webster record-batch 8` three separate times with the same `batch_failed` cause.
Each time the implementer fork ran `go run ./tools/tokencount -last 40 -calibrate cautious -history <sibling fabric repo path>`, and the audit reported:

`fabric-reference violation ... ran a fabric-referencing command (...) that can rewrite run state — an implementer fork must never touch the fabric repo directly`

Each failure was followed by `lyx webster recover-batch 8`, which refused with `needs_fresh: true` ("batch 08 failed on findings recovery cannot check: fabric-reference ... (the finding names no path)").
The webster master then escalated to the human each time, so the loom run halted as `blocked` (anomaly `escalation-to-human`) three times.
A driver re-step after a `lyx` binary change (`last_step.binary_changed`) respawned the master, which asked again for the same cause, so the new build did not change the outcome.

## Why it is abnormal

- The fork repeats the same command in every attempt, so whatever instructs it (batch brief or plan) and the audit disagree; no attempt can pass, and the loop is only broken by a human.
- The audit treats any command mentioning the fabric path as one that "can rewrite run state", without distinguishing a read-only calibration invocation, and the finding carries no path, so `recover-batch` cannot verify it and refuses.
- The `recover-batch` refusal's way forward is inconsistent between attempts: the first offered only `reset --to start` then `run --fresh`, the later ones also offered `accept-audit --batch 8` then `recover-batch 8` (when the batch made no commit and the worktree is clean).
  A batch that failed only on an audit finding should say up front which of these applies.

## What to do

- Decide whether `tools/tokencount` with `-history` is a legitimate implementer-fork command; if so, whitelist read-only tokencount calibration in the fabric-reference audit, or make the batch brief tell the fork not to run it.
- Make the audit explain what the fork should do instead, and have `recover-batch` offer `accept-audit` consistently whenever it is applicable.
- Consider a halt that repeats the identical audit finding to be surfaced as one escalation with the cause, rather than three master questions.

Provenance: task `card-batching`; notes `webster-refusal-record-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-record-batch-2.md`, `webster-refusal-record-batch-3.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch-2.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch-3.md`, `loom-halt.md`, `loom-halt-2.md`, `loom-halt-3.md`, `driver-binary-change-restep-20261007.md`.


## From issue #432

Imported from [issue #432](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/432).

## What happened

A webster batch (`13-tail-in-stencils-and-steer`) needed run-event data that lives under the weft checkout's `.lyx/shuttle/*/events.jsonl`.
The implementer fork read those files with read-only shell commands (`head`, `jq`, `awk`, `cat`, `grep`).
`lyx webster record-batch 13` failed the batch with a fabric-reference violation for each such command ("can rewrite run state — an implementer fork must never touch the fabric repo directly").
The batch's card did not say which route to the data is allowed, so the fork had no way to know the reads would be flagged.

The way forward then looped:

1. `lyx webster recover-batch 13` refused: "batch 13 failed on findings recovery cannot check", with `needs_fresh: true` and the finding "names no path".
   It was run twice with the identical refusal.
2. The refusal pointed to `lyx webster accept-audit --batch 13` followed by `recover-batch`, valid only when the batch made no commit.
3. `lyx webster accept-audit --batch=13` refused: "batch 13 made a commit or recorded no start commit, so its tree cannot be shown unchanged"; its way forward is `lyx webster reset --to start` and `lyx webster run --fresh`.

The batch had committed work, so the only remaining route was discarding the batch.
A recovery strand later read the same files read-only through the worktrees' own `.lyx` links (which name no weft path) and the audit passed, so the route was found by trial.

## Why it is abnormal

- The audit classifies commands that only read run files as ones that "can rewrite run state"; a read-only `head`/`jq`/`cat` of an events file is not a rewrite.
- The finding carries no path, so `recover-batch` cannot verify it and demands a fresh run, and `accept-audit` is unusable once the batch has committed.
  A finding that is a false positive on a committed batch has no accept route.
- Nothing tells an implementer (card, prompt or audit message) which access route to run files is permitted.

## What to do

- Make the fabric-reference audit distinguish read-only commands from ones that write, or name the allowed read route in the implementer prompt/card.
- Let `accept-audit` (or `recover-batch`) handle a finding on a batch that committed, for example by checking that the commit does not touch the fabric repo, instead of requiring an unchanged tree.
- Give the finding a path (or the command's target) so recovery can check it.

Provenance: task `shuttle-turns`; notes `webster-refusal-record-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch-2.md`, `webster-refusal-accept-audit.md`, `13-tail-in-stencils-and-steer-recovery.md`.

entries.title: A Webster stuck outcome is reported as the master asking a question
entries.brief: loom said webster master is asking a question when the master had written outcome: stuck and ended its turn
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-07 in card-batching: the batten notice and loom status said `webster master is asking a question`, but the master had written `_lyx/webster/outcome.yaml` with `outcome: stuck` plus `summary.md` and ended its turn. The stop must be classified from the outcome file, not as a question; see `session-state` for the wider model.

## From issue #429

Imported from [issue #429](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/429).

**What happened**

During the Webster row, Master delegated a batch to a fork that ran a long after-state measurement in a background shell.
Master's turn ended with only interim fork output, because it was holding `record-batch` until the fork's final completion notification.
lyx's wait ran past `background_shell_wait_min` (10 minutes), stopped waiting and counted Master's turn end.
It did not stop the shell.
The run's outcome became `error: webster: master asked a question instead of finishing`, and the loom halted `blocked` with anomaly `escalation-to-human`.

Friction notes reported "Master's wait counted a turn end past a background shell" twice, in two different Master sessions.
The driver re-stepped the Webster row after a binary change (`last_step.binary_changed`) and Master blocked the same way a second time, still waiting on the same fork's measurement.
The halt recurred, so one re-step does not clear it.

**Why this is abnormal**

An interim "still waiting on a background job" turn end is not a question to a human, and halting the loom as `escalation-to-human` for it needs an operator for no reason.
The wait gives up on the shell after a fixed time, but the shell and the Master strand stay alive until the next `lyx webster run` reclaims them, so the work being waited on is killed or orphaned on the very re-step meant to recover.
The log line "stopping a leftover live strand before respawning it; an in-flight batch run restarts from state.json rather than resuming" shows the re-step discards the pending wait.

**What to do**

- Do not classify a Master turn end that is waiting on a live fork or background shell as a question or an `error`.
- Either keep waiting while the fork's background job is live, or resume Master when the job completes, instead of halting.
- If giving up after `background_shell_wait_min` stays, stop the shell and surface a distinct anomaly, not `escalation-to-human`.

Provenance: task `test-tiers`; notes `webster-background-shell.md`, `webster-background-shell-2.md`, `loom-halt.md`, `loom-halt-2.md`, `driver-restep-20261007-webster-blocked.md`.

entries.title: Batcher v2: Merriam context at fork time, a fitted model, plans in card order
entries.brief: Size batches from Merriam measured context, fit the batchifier from logged runs, one tokencount weft flag, card order in the plan spec
entries.body:
Card batching (landed 2026-10-07) cut Webster's time and tokens visibly; this task makes its model measured instead of guessed.

## Merriam's context at fork time

Operator, 2026-10-07: the cost batchifier's `startup_context` (60000 in the `cautious` profile) is a fitted constant standing in for something that is not constant.

An implementer fork is a fork of Merriam, so it starts with Merriam's whole context at the moment it is spawned, and that context grows with every finished batch.
A constant is too high for early batches and too low for late batches of a long plan, which is where a large batch can overrun the budget.

The start context of batch N is Merriam's base context plus a growth term for batches 1 to N−1.

- Base: computable exactly before the run, since it is fixed by what Merriam loads: Claude Code's system prompt and tools, CLAUDE.md, the Webster stencil with the inlined PATTERN overview, and the plan files Merriam reads.
- Growth: what comes back between forks, the batch reports and the output of Merriam's `lyx webster` verbs; estimated, for example as a per-card or per-report allowance.

The partition stays computed once per run, as `webster-spec.md` requires.

Measure first: read Merriam's actual context at each fork from its transcript in the runs that used the `cautious` profile (`shuttle-turns`, `test-tiers`, `run-recovery`), to size the base and the growth term and to see how far the constant was off.
Compare weight per card in those runs against earlier identity-batchifier runs with `tools/tokencount`.

## Learning loop

Operator, 2026-10-07: the batchifier's model is a first guess; treat tuning as a learning loop rather than a design-time decision.

- Log: each batch records its profile, coefficients and per-card estimate components in webster's `state.json`; the fork transcripts give the actual peak context (max input+cache tokens of any message) and the actual weight.
- Analyse: extend `tools/tokencount -calibrate` to read those records from finished runs and fit the peak-context coefficients (estimate vs actual peak) and the cost side (weight per batch vs batch size).
- Decide on data: the batch size and budget that minimise weight per card without a rise in failed batches, recoveries or Webster-Review findings; quality outcomes (batch failed, recover-batch, review findings per card) belong in the same table.
- Re-fit as runs accumulate, and compare profiles across runs before changing the default.

## One flag for the weft repository

`tools/tokencount` has both `-weft` (finished runs) and `-history` (calibration) naming the same weft repository; one flag with one default would do.

## Plans run in card order

Rule (operator, 2026-10-06): a valid plan is executable strictly in card-number order; a card never depends on anything a later card does, and Webster follows that order as written and never sorts cards.

Plan-Gate refuses backward dependencies since `bugfix-webster` (`uses-later-target`, `delete-before-reference`), and card-batching made the batchifier's contiguous segments in card order the execution order.
Still open: `contracts/specs/loom-plan-spec.md` calls the card list a DAG of intent "not itself an execution order", and the plan template does not tell the writer the rule.
Both state it, to the plan writer and the plan reviewer, so Plan-Write stops bouncing on plans Webster used to reorder.

entries.title: Burler: a parallel reviewer and fixer, a model per round
entries.brief: Split a Burler round into a cheap reviewer and a stronger fixer that start together, and pick the model per round
entries.body:
Both halves aim at the cost and time of a Burler round.

## Split a round into reviewer and fixer

Idea (operator, 2026-10-03): split a Burler round into two agents spawned in parallel.

- **A, handler and fixer**, the stronger model.
- **B, reviewer**, writes the review only and never fixes.

Both start at once and orient themselves in the code independently.
B then forks its lens fan as today, and when every fork is done, writes the combined report as Burler does now.
The report goes to A, which has already oriented itself, fixes, and acts as an extra validator that takes B's findings with a grain of salt.

What it buys: A's orientation overlaps B's review instead of following it, and the reviewer never grades its own fixes.

Models (operator, 2026-10-07): the review half, one agent forking a lens each into a broad review, is good enough on `sonnet[medium]`; the fixer and validator is the one that must be stronger.
Today one agent does both under the single `review` model-spec in `loom.yaml`, so they cannot be set apart; the split gives each half its own model-spec.
Seen 2026-10-07 in `bugfix-fabric`: on `sonnet[medium]` the fix half cleared only the lines a review named, re-broke a line fixed the round before, and circled through rounds 3 and 4 on comment line breaks alone; `review` was raised to `opus[medium]` for both halves as a stopgap.

## A model per round

From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday (shuttle per-round provider selector), reframed by the operator on 2026-10-03: Burler chooses a different base model for round 1, round 2 and later rounds, so a fresh model reviews after the first has converged.
Related: `convergence-plan`'s model trial (`fable[high]` for discussion and review).
